Breaking: The Hunger Games: Sunrise On The Reaping Has A Unique Credit You Rarely See In Movies

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (607 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Slashfilm

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that suzanne Collins is the engine that drives the "Hunger Games" franchise.
  • Sources indicate that "Sunrise on the Reaping" ruled the box office on its opening weekend, meaning that quite a few people might have noticed that once the credits roll, there's some text reading, "Adaptation by Suzanne Collins." So, while Billy Ray and Michael Lesslie are credited with the movie's screenplay, Collins got credit for the adaptation of her 2024 book of the same name.
  • "In the interest of avoiding a multiplicity of credits, the Guild is opposed to the general use of the 'Adaptation by' credit," the Writers Guild of America's screen credits manual states.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that suzanne Collins is the engine that drives the "Hunger Games" franchise. As the author behind the books, none of the movies happen without her. Beyond that, though, Collins has remained very close to the adaptations of her work, with Lionsgate consulting with her every step of the way. That's especially true with the franchise's latest prequel film, "The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping" — so much so that it resulted in a unique credit we rarely see in movies.

Sources indicate that "Sunrise on the Reaping" ruled the box office on its opening weekend, meaning that quite a few people might have noticed that once the credits roll, there's some text reading, "Adaptation by Suzanne Collins." So, while Billy Ray and Michael Lesslie are credited with the movie's screenplay, Collins got credit for the adaptation of her 2024 book of the same name. This is exceptionally rare in Hollywood.

"In the interest of avoiding a multiplicity of credits, the Guild is opposed to the general use of the 'Adaptation by' credit," the Writers Guild of America's screen credits manual states. But that doesn't mean it never gets used, and "Sunrise on the Reaping" warranted its rare usage. The manual further explains:.

According to recent reports, "The Guild recognizes that there are certain unusual cases where credit is due a writer who shapes the direction of screenplay construction without qualifying for 'Screenplay by' credit. In those special cases, and only as a result of arbitration, the 'Adaptation by' credit may be used.".

Who gets credit for a screenplay can be difficult to actually pin down. In the movie business, it's rare that it's literally just one person writing a script and that's that. It's why Joss Whedon wasn't credited for his writing work on "Speed." It's also why Collins nabbed this unique credit.

Arbitration is a process used primarily to determine writing credits. As the WGA manual states, arbitration is usually the only way that this "Adaptation by" credit winds up being used. That doesn't mean that things got contentious between Billy Ray, Michael Lesslie, and Suzanne Collins, it's just a unique situation.

It has been revealed that collins generally feels happy with the "Hunger Games" movie adaptations and even co-wrote the first movie personally. By all accounts, she has a good relationship with Lionsgate, director Francis Lawrence, and other key creatives. The fact that she wound up with this rare credit, if anything, reflects her level of involvement.

Speaking with The Hollywood Reporter, Ray offered a window into the collaboration, explaining that he communicated very directly with Collins when it came to determining how to adapt her latest book for the screen:.

In a recent development, "At the very beginning of the process, I asked Suzanne, 'What is this book about for you?' She talked about the philosophy of the book: the philosophy of propaganda and implicit submission, the philosophy of Thomas Hobbes, David Hume, and John Locke. And I noted, 'Suzanne, what's the book about for you emotionally?' She said, 'It's about love and loss.' I said, 'Great, that's what I'm writing.' So, anything that didn't stick to that had to go.".

In many cases, the writer of a book is left out in the cold when it comes to that book being turned into a movie. But not in this case. The few changes "Sunrise on the Reaping" makes to its source material don't appear to be against Collins' wishes. She was being consulted behind the scenes the whole way and was credited as such.

"The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping" is in theaters now.

How to get your car out of the impound in GTA 6

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It doesn't take long for one of your cars to end up at the police impound in Grand Theft Auto 6.
  • If you are not ready to abandon your favorite car and want it back, we've got you covered.
  • In a recent development, there are two methods to retrieve a car from the police impound: you can either steal it back or pay for it.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It doesn't take long for one of your cars to end up at the police impound in Grand Theft Auto 6. You might have abandoned it near a crime scene, or they arrested you while you were driving it. While the circumstances may vary, you have only two ways to proceed if a car is impounded: you forget about it or you retrieve it.

If you are not ready to abandon your favorite car and want it back, we've got you covered. Here's how to get your car out of the impound in GTA 6.

In a recent development, there are two methods to retrieve a car from the police impound: you can either steal it back or pay for it. Both are valid, but the second one becomes available only in Chapter 2.

According to recent reports, stealing the car is the most plausible and cheapest option to execute. You just need to head to the impound lot, enter, and drive your car away from there. Some impounds, like the one in Port Gellhorn, have openings that you can use to enter unnoticed. Regardless of how you get inside, the challenge is escaping from the police once you leave. You must be prepared to run away, so try to come up with an escape route by setting a destination far from the city.

Now, the second option requires the Scooter Bros app, which you unlock in Chapter 2 after completing Moses' mission. If you have it already, open the app and select the impounded car (the one with a police badge icon). You will see that the first option in the menu is to pay a fee to retrieve the car.

The price varies depending on how far you are from the police impound. For example, I would have to pay $699 to get my car back from the Port Gellhorn impound while in Vice City. However, if you have upgraded your Scooter Bros account to Premium, you can use your remaining daily credits to request an impounded vehicle. Since this will essentially consume all your credits for the day, you should wait until you have only one left before using this option.

There's a set of explainers for GTA 6's more open-ended side activities, like how to rob the Exotic Animal Front and where to find tree effigies for the Skunk Ape mission, and we've got all the GTA 6 cheat codes. You'll have to put in some effort before you can use those, though.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that the Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth is the first time in nearly a decade that audiences can see acclaimed filmmaker Quentin Tarantino's work in theaters.
  • Brad Pitt once again plays Cliff Booth, who now finds himself in 1977 without the trusty Rick Dalton by his side.
  • ScreenRant's Kim Horcher interviewed Caan, Debicki, Gugino, and Abdul-Mateen about the exciting challenge of stepping into Tarantino's world through the lens of Fincher's camera in The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that the Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth is the first time in nearly a decade that audiences can see acclaimed filmmaker Quentin Tarantino's work in theaters. While the sequel to 2019's love letter to American cinema, Once Upon a Time in... Hollywood, was directed by David Fincher, Tarantino still penned the screenplay. The combination of both powerhouses has made the movie one of the year's most anticipated, and the cast even felt the magic while working on set.

Brad Pitt once again plays Cliff Booth, who now finds himself in 1977 without the trusty Rick Dalton by his side. While he is no longer at the center of Hollywood, he still hangs out with famous folk within the industry, doing their dirty work in the seedy underbelly of Los Angeles. He runs into various fascinating characters, including actor Charlie Peters (Scott Caan), whose tension with his wife Toni (Carla Gugino) becomes central to the plot. Charlie's agent, Karen Crosby (Elizabeth Debicki), finds herself entangled with Cliff romantically, while Blaxploitation movie star Roderick "Hot Rod" Harrison (Yahya Abdul-Mateen II) adds plenty of charm to the proceedings.

ScreenRant's Kim Horcher interviewed Caan, Debicki, Gugino, and Abdul-Mateen about the exciting challenge of stepping into Tarantino's world through the lens of Fincher's camera in The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth. The actors shared their reactions to joining the project, how they got into character, and which they found to be the best parts of fictional 1970s Hollywood.

Industry observers note that screenRant: How was it working with Fincher on a Tarantino project? How did it feel to get that call?

In a recent development, carla Gugino: It's pretty much the best call you could ever get, honestly. I think it's almost as simple as that. You have the foundation of this incredible script, and then you have one of the greatest visionary directors interpreting it through his lens. And that combination is so unique. I don't know that we'll ever get that kind of combination. It's such an unusual opportunity. It's like falling into a pot of honey.

According to recent reports, yahya Abdul-Mateen II: It makes the job easy. We both have a theater background. When I go to do theater, I get a chance to say the best words, and that helps a lot. We had everything that we needed in order to succeed, and so the stage was set for us to just bring the best of ourselves without having to figure out how to make things work so much, which sometimes is what we have to do.

The job is to figure out how to make things work. But sometimes when you have to do that less, then you can just get in there, and it's just about what you get to do. "Ooh, I get to do this." That's what work felt like on most days for me. I felt like a star.

This project was a gift, a throwback to a really, really fun time. And to make a present-day movie that is a '70s movie with the flair of Quentin Tarantino's words, and under the direction of David Fincher's eye with Brad and the entire cast? It was just really, really fun.

Carla Gugino: I think the thing about Quentin's writing that's so noticeable is that nothing is ever generic. You really believe these people are real people. It's a lot like Elmore Leonard, where they act in unexpected ways. When most people are nervous, they're flirty. He brings the period to life in a really exceptional way.

According to recent reports, and then David is so known for how impeccable he is with period stuff, so I [love] the fact that we got to embody this world of the '70s and what it represents. There's this star, and we have a stunt guy who is kind of in awe of that star. We have a lifelong actress who's made a living that way, but hasn't been as successful as she wants to be, but also is kind of okay with that. Then we have a TV star who gets a taste of all the different elements of Hollywood at that time. Everybody is sort of compromised, and that's kind of what the '70s was like in a lot of ways. So, all those things are very noticeable.

Recent findings suggest that screenRant: Elizabeth, your character really surprised me with her somewhat contradictory nature and her multidimensionality. I feel like I've met people like her in LA. What was she to you?

It has been revealed that elizabeth Debicki: She was an amazing role that I found in that script. I think Quentin created a character that is quite unlike anything else he's written for a female character. She is really contradictory, and I think that is the core of human nature. We just roam around and contradict ourselves.

It has been revealed that she obviously has real agency in this world, but she's really smart and funny and completely not ready for someone to walk into her life to kind of force her to look at herself. It's a really interesting relationship between her and Cliff, and I loved playing her.

In a recent development, when David and I first spoke about it, I remember us both saying our goal really was that we really wanted her to feel real, like someone you knew. I wanted her to feel like, "I know that woman. I wonder what she ate for breakfast. I bet she lives in an apartment that looks like that." She feels grounded.

Industry observers note that screenRant: Scott, on the other hand, I feel like I've only met maybe one or two Charlies. What went into making him your own?

Scott Caan: Listen, Quentin writes really great characters, and when I read the script, I was like, "Wow, this one is fantastic." For me, I like to bring as much of myself into the character as I can. For this one, initially, it was like, "God, how do I justify all this stuff?" That was really my approach. "How can I justify all my behavior and all these decisions?" And it was very fun.

Industry observers note that there's one [actor he reminded me of], which I'm not even going to mention who it is, but there was one idea. We were talking about it before, but it kind of went away. We do a lot of homework, and then when you show up, you kind of forget it all and just go try to play. I mean, the guy's got to be a version of me. So, I read something, and I go, "Alright, how can I put the version of me into this?".

The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth begins playing in select IMAX theaters on November 25 before streaming December 23 on Netflix.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Of all days on the broadcast television schedule, Super Bowl Sunday has always held a coveted status. The big game itself is always a cultural moment that routinely draws in hundreds of millions of viewers to see the culmination of the NFL season live, with all the bells and whistles attached. However, it's also a crucial day for whatever series gets to air in the immediate aftermath and benefit from the colossal lead-in. Networks in the past have typically used the spot for newly introduced series they've felt confident about and special episodes of ratings darlings, with everything from The Office to The Late Show with Stephen Colbert and Survivor airing afterward. This year, with ABC hosting the festivities, it will be the latter.

Recent findings suggest that after being held for the midseason for the first time since its debut in 2024, High Potential will be making up for lost time with a special Season 3 episode right after the Super Bowl on February 14. The Kaitlin Olson-led crime drama will regularly air on Tuesdays, starting on January 5, but the bonus time slot will be utilized to give the series a massive spotlight and allow fresh showrunners and Scream 8 writers Nora and Lilla Zuckerman to get creative with Morgan Gillory and the LAPD. Taking a page from the last time they hosted the big game in 2006, with Grey's Anatomy getting the lead-in, ABC will be airing the first piece of a two-part storyline with a cliffhanger that will be resolved on February 16. Plot details are unknown at this time.

In a recent development, high Potential was about a slam dunk to earn the coveted lead-in for the network's first Super Bowl in a decade. It finished the 2025/2026 broadcast season pacing all broadcast television programs in the key demographic of adults 18-49 and ranking third in overall 35-day multiplatform viewing with over 16.01 million tuning in on average. That came after it went toe-to-toe with CBS' ever-popular Tracker for the title of most-watched network series of 2025. Enough viewers have fallen in love with Morgan and her unconventional crime-solving ways to make the series a suitably buzzy pick to follow up the biggest sporting event of the year in the U.S.

In a recent development, A great detective is really just a personality with a method attached, which is why we keep remaking the same four of them. Here is yours, what it says about you, and the case for them being the best in the business.

You let people think you are not a threat and then you simply never go away. Columbo is the only major detective show that tells you who did it in the first ten minutes, because the pleasure was never the puzzle, it was watching a rich man slowly realise he is in trouble.

You are the most interesting person in the room and you know exactly how to use it. Rian Johnson built Blanc as a gentleman detective who is also an outsider everywhere he goes, which lets him be charming at people who would never otherwise talk to him.

Everybody tells you everything, and you have never once asked them to. Jessica Fletcher is a crime novelist from a small town in Maine who is so warm and so obviously trustworthy that suspects confess to her essentially as a social courtesy.

In a recent development, you expect to be lied to and you are almost never disappointed. Chandler wrote Marlowe as a man with a rigid private code in a city that has none, which is why he takes the case, solves it, gets nothing out of it and takes the next one.

Created by Drew Goddard, High Potential has seen Morgan rise from an LAPD cleaner with an IQ of 160 to a trusted civilian consultant of the Major Crimes Division, using her intellect to solve the crimes that vex the police. Her unique approach makes her the surprisingly perfect partner for the by-the-books detective Karadec (Daniel Sunjata), whose own methods tend to run up against the sleuth's. Season 3 will pick up after a climactic finale that saw Captain Wagner (Steve Howey) left on death's door by a gunshot and Morgan's missing husband, Roman, potentially visit their daughter's art show under the cloak of secrecy. As such, Howey will be sitting out this season, but Javicia Leslie joins Olson and Sunjata among the returning cast, alongside Deniz Akdeniz, Amirah J, Matthew Lamb, and Judy Reyes rounding out the bunch.

It has been revealed that high Potential Season 3 premieres on January 5. Stay tuned here at Collider.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A very successful “values-based entertainment” organization that was begat — in the parlance of its biblical heritage — from a film-filtering service that illegally edited “objectionable content” out of major Hollywood movies, Angel Studios has since become the world’s foremost purveyor of megachurch-approved multiplex content. The bigger they got (on the strength of projects like “The Chosen” and the QAnon cause célèbre “Sound of Freedom,” the latter of which pioneered a questionable ticketing model that continues today), the more that Angel removed from the films they released. Not just sex and swear words, but also anything that even vaguely resembled a soul. Related Stories Billy Ray Joins Oscar Short Contender ‘Magan’s Fare,’ Starring Barkhad Abdi, as Executive Producer Why Is the ‘Avengers: Doomsday’ Trailer So… Gloomy? Internet Erupts Over Latest Look at Marvel Movie.

With “Hershey,” a decidedly vanilla biopic about the most famous chocolatier who’s ever lived, the studio has taken its socio-religious project to its logical conclusion: They’ve made a movie that’s been stripped of any flavor whatsoever. It’s the cinematic equivalent of carob powder. It’s what Ned Flanders will force his kids to watch next Halloween.

Industry observers note that somehow unimaginatively bland and Splenda-sweet all at once, this godforsaken affront to good storytelling may not have benefited from any of the material that its distributor has deemed amoral, but “Hershey” is so mind-numbingly absent the most basic friction of the human experience that I wanted to fall to my knees and thank the lord that a few errant Kisses made it past The Angel Promise on a technicality. It’s too bad Milton S. Hershey never used his platform to baselessly sow doubt in a foreign election, because at least one of Angel Studios’ co-founders would clearly have been cool with including that (ecocidal fascism is fine, just don’t say “fuck” while you’re razing the Amazon, as that would offend Jesus).

As you may have gathered by now, I am probably not the target audience for this unrepentant godslop.

Industry observers note that not because I’m agnostic (“Hershey” is as secular as Angel Studios’ output gets, its overt religiosity limited to a brief scene in which the movie’s namesake pleads for help from an unspecified higher power), but rather because I stubbornly, blasphemously insist that a womb-to-tomb biopic should bear at least some faint resemblance to the stuff of real life. I couldn’t possibly care less about the facts (though I struggle to believe that Hershey and his wife literally danced with joy after learning that a twist of fate had spared them from being aboard the Titanic), but there isn’t a single moment in this film that feels like it was written by a real person, let alone lived by one.

It has been revealed that let’s back up a beat. To be clear, Angel Studios didn’t technically make this movie — that distinction belongs to the spiritually aligned production organization Dandelion Media, who partnered with Hershey Entities for a fully authorized feature-length commercial meant to “bring [the chocolate brand’s] story into culture in a more immersive way.” The success of that marketing spend remains to be seen, but it can’t hurt to highlight Mr. Hershey’s ostensible purity at a time when the company that bears his name has been under fire for diluting its products with compound coatings in order to save money. And so we have a punishingly straightforward film that paints the Pennsylvania icon as a square-jawed, sweet-toothed wife guy who loved candy, orphans, and sitting way too close to the edge of the massive water tower that overlooks the town he remade in his own image.

Directed by Mark Waters, but absent any trace of the poppy confidence he once brought to the likes of “Mean Girls” and “Freaky Friday,” “Hershey” opens with its first and only stylistic flourish as a match cut transforms an immaculate chocolate Kiss into a small lump of coal — Milton Hershey’s life would turn out to be sweet, but it sure didn’t start that way. The film that follows sadly feels less like “Lawrence of Arabia” than it does an AI-generated adaptation of Hershey’s Wikipedia page, its algorithmic sense of human interaction rendered all the more uncanny by its ecclesiastical approach to conflict (and also by its blown out cinematography, which suggests a very literal interpretation of Angel Studios’ promise to produce “movies and highlights that amplify light.”).

Adhering to the prosaic structure and candied morality that the Erwin brothers have made endemic to the world of faith-based biopics and their immediate kin, the film sees Hershey’s life as a blessed march towards his eternal reward — one that’s only slowed down by the litany of speed bumps that pop up along his path to heaven.

Young Milton’s very serious Mennonite mom is a major bummer, but she lets him out of the house to work for a local printer. The JRPG-like town where he grows up in the 1860s seems inhospitable to dreams, but its muddy roads make it appear as though the streets are paved with chocolate. His dad (Alan Ruck, a long way from “Succession”) abandons him pretty fast, but not before bending down to the kid like Zooey Deschanel in “Almost Famous” and telling him: “You’re a Hershey, and that means when you follow your dream, you don’t let anyone get in your way.” Apparently his dad’s dream was to not live with his family anymore, but so be it. A good example is a good example.

It has been revealed that every stumbling block is immediately followed by a burst of divine providence, as Sharon Paul and Timothy Michael Hayes’ script adheres to the grindset mindset of the prosperity gospel while Rolfe Kent’s saccharine score blends everything together into a tasteless slurry of unrefined sugar. The film insists that a little sweetness goes a long way, as an orgasmic taste of rock candy is all that Milton needs to make it through the day, but it doesn’t heed its own advice. Milton’s passion leads him to a job working for a saintly confectioner named Joseph Royer (a beneficent Richard Kind, as close to a live-action Bing Bong as he’s ever been), who just smiles it off when the kid forgets to turn off the peanut roaster and nearly burns down the whole shop.

Industry observers note that later, after sprouting into Finn Wittrock and starting his own caramel organization, Milton is miraculously spared from ruin several times over by virtue of his non-denominational faith in himself and the universe. One low moment is redeemed by a massive order from overseas. Another resolves with a traveling salesman busting into the Lancaster Caramel Company with an offer to invest in chocolate — the future of snacking! “This chocolate,” Milton sniffs, “it could be good if it wasn’t so bad.” I know the feeling. The next time disaster strikes, he inadvertently stumbles upon the Hershey Kiss in the very next scene. The plotting is schematic enough to make “Bohemian Rhapsody” seem like “Last Days” by comparison.

Somewhere in there Milton enjoys a meet-cute with a woman named Kitty Sweeney (Alexandria Daddario), a grinning beauty who credits caramels with curing her shyness. Her job as Milton’s wife is to be his biggest cheerleader, and then — as the years melt away — to collapse in undiagnosed pain whenever he leaves the room. At one point it is implied that she and Milton have sexual intercourse, but only so the movie can leverage the couple’s inability to conceive a child into a robust philanthropic regime that allowed them to house and educate any number of white male orphans.

According to recent reports, of course, expecting this movie to acknowledge the Milton Hershey School’s history of racial and social discrimination would be as delusional as thinking its third act might address the labor disputes that unsettled Hershey’s chocolate factory in the late 1930s. Such things are simply not sweet enough to befit a story about how some vague belief and a little stick-it-to-em are all a man needs to prosper in this great land — even if a warts-and-all version of that same story would still be a model of American success.

Considerably less textured than the chocolate bars that have become synonymous with its title character, Waters’ film is so determined to launder one man’s dreams into reality that it comes to assume its own kind of dream logic in return — one divorced from the basic relationship between cause-and-effect or an event and its meaning.

In what might be the single most deranged movie scene of the year, Milton and his ailing wife Kitty literally dance for joy on the bow of a ship after learning that a twist of fate has spared them from being aboard the Titanic, even though upwards of 1,400 other people went to a watery grave that night. I’m not sure that qualifies as bringing the brand’s “story into the culture in a more immersive way,” but it’s definitely what I’m going to be thinking about the next time I bite into a milky and delicious Hershey Bar. After watching this perversely chalky film about the firm’s founder, it’s a wonder that I can still remember what their signature product even tastes like.

Angel Studios will release “Hershey” in theaters on Wednesday, November 25.

Tech Report: Vice City portal Easter egg location in GTA 6

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (933 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Polygon

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that the Vice City portal Easter egg is a unique event in Grand Theft Auto 6 that lets you travel through time.
  • To experience this event and open the portal, you will have to complete a long series of steps.
  • If you want to start the Vice City portal event in GTA 6, you must travel to Key Lento, the initial area in the game, and head to the Badger radio tower, northeast of the Nifty Threads Island Wear shop.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that the Vice City portal Easter egg is a unique event in Grand Theft Auto 6 that lets you travel through time. It might not look like it, but the existence of a secret portal in Leonida is quite plausible, considering the UFOs appearing in the skies and the forgotten haunted hotels you can visit.

To experience this event and open the portal, you will have to complete a long series of steps. But don't worry, below, we explain everything you need to know to complete the Vice City portal Easter egg in GTA 6.

If you want to start the Vice City portal event in GTA 6, you must travel to Key Lento, the initial area in the game, and head to the Badger radio tower, northeast of the Nifty Threads Island Wear shop. Enter the tower and climb to the top to reach what appears to be a control room.

In a recent development, beside the door, there's a lever. Pull it up then press the button on the panel near the old television. If you've done everything correctly, the TV will turn on and display the word "Malibu." Now, leave the tower and prepare for the next step.

Industry observers note that after you have finished the initial ratio tower step, you will need to visit 12 LPL substations around Leonidas following a specific order. There will be a letter or two on the outer wall of each substation, which will form a secret message when all 12 letters are put together. In each one, you will find either a button or a lever that represents a letter or symbol. To ensure you're interacting with the correct one, check the pink tape near the button/lever and look for the letter/symbol it features.

Before you start, keep in mind that you can't fast travel using the RydeMe app or swap between characters. Doing so resets the mission, and you will need to return to the radio tower to start it again. You'll know that you have completed this step when you receive a message from an unknown contact after you pull up the last lever. Below, we listed the substations in the order you must visit them, where you will find the button or lever you must activate, and which letter they represent.

Location: Vice City (Vice-Dale County) — Southwest corner of Downtown, just southwest of Zenith gym.

Location: Vice City (Vice-Dale County) — West side of Balsero, just northwest of Randy's shop.

Location: Key Lento (Mariana County) —Northwest of Kenton's shop.

Location: Vice Beach (Vice-Dale County) — North side of Penmarch Isle.

Location: Vice City (Vice-Dale County) — West side of Bayside, just northwest of the Vice City apartment.

Location: Port Gellhorn (Kelly County) — North of Moses' shop.

Location: Hamlet (Vice-Dale County) — East of Massive Shot Ammu-Nation shop​​​​​​​.

Location: Vice City (Vice-Dale County) — Northwest area of Gloriana Key.

Location: Hamlet (Vice-Dale County) - East side of Hamlet, just northeast of the Boone Speedway.

Location: Gellhorn (Kelly County) — Northeast of Raceway.

Location: Hamlet (Vice-Dale County) - South side of Hamlet, just southeast of Boone Speedway and the Pay 'N' Spray.

Location: North Mariana County (Mariana County) — South of Breakwater Quarry.

If you combine all the letters, you'll get the message: Life is passing me by, which is a PC cheat code that allows you to speed up time in Grand Theft Auto: Vice City.

The final step in the event requires you to follow the instructions in the message you receive after activating the 12th lever: head to the T. H. Power Station, east of Hamlet in Vice-Dale County, between 7 p.m. and 6 a.m. Once there, you will find the portal that will take you to the original Vice City.

You can find the portal on the north side of the power station. You'll know you're at the right place if you can see traces of energy from the portal running through the cables in the area. Reaching the portal might be difficult, considering how heavily guarded the area is. Consider either using a helicopter or swimming around the area to find a good entry point.

In a recent development, once you find the portal, pull the lever on the left side of the gate, and you'll be teleported. To leave the original Vice City, just head to the room behind the bar, and you will be back to the world of GTA 6. By completing this event, you will receive Tony Vercetti's Hawaiian shirt, the American Glory motorcycle (don't forget to register it!), and unlock a upcoming livery for purchase at Vice Vinyl.

If you're just getting started in GTA 6, we have plenty of guides to help you live the high life in Leonida. Check out our GTA 6 beginner guide to get a grasp of the basics and our tips for what to do first, recommendations for the best ways to make money fast, and an explainer for how to keep stolen weapons and cars to make the most of your free time.

Industry observers note that our selection of GTA 6 guides includes help for things like how to steal the Phoenix in "Unwanted Attention" and whether you should defuse Mandy, too. There's a set of explainers for GTA 6's more open-ended side activities, like how to rob the Exotic Animal Front and where to find tree effigies for the Skunk Ape mission, and we've got all the GTA 6 cheat codes. You'll have to put in some effort before you can use those, though.

#85590. The Mosquito Bowl Won’t Let You Forget What It’s Really About

📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 18m • 📚 Deep Dive (3626 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Screenrant ↗ Open Full Page

The Mosquito Bowl Won’t Let You Forget What It’s Really About

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 18 min read (3626 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Screenrant

⏱️ ~18 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that on Christmas Eve in 1944, on the Pacific island of Guadalcanal, two regiments of US Marines training for the invasion of Okinawa played a game of football.
  • Industry observers note that I can assure you, you have not.
  • "The goal of the movie was to grab the audience by the throat and make them feel something," Berg told ScreenRant's Liam Crowley in an interview alongside Bissinger.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that on Christmas Eve in 1944, on the Pacific island of Guadalcanal, two regiments of US Marines training for the invasion of Okinawa played a game of football. That game is, ostensibly, the subject of The Mosquito Bowl, the new film from director Peter Berg that will be available to stream on Netflix from November 25, as well as the 2022 nonfiction book by Buzz Bissinger that inspired it. Considering the pairing of Berg and Bissinger once yielded Friday Night Lights, you might feel like you've heard enough to know what you're in for.

Industry observers note that I can assure you, you have not. The Mosquito Bowl is in some ways about football – it is certainly about a handful of football players – but it's really a movie about war, and everything war costs. It follows four young men with hopes, dreams, and plenty of talent on the gridiron, who are diverted from whatever paths their lives may have taken and sent into a world of horrific violence and death. A world that is quite shockingly depicted.

"The goal of the movie was to grab the audience by the throat and make them feel something," Berg told ScreenRant's Liam Crowley in an interview alongside Bissinger. "To make something that feels like a participatory experience, not a spectator experience. I've had people see this film, and after it's like, 'Jesus Christ, I need to just go be quiet.'".

For this ScreenRant Cover Story, Berg and Bissinger talked us through what went into The Mosquito Bowl to create such a gripping watch, from its relationship to the true story and the real people that lived it to the quartet of actors and practical filmmaking that brought their experience to life.

Industry observers note that peter Berg and Buzz Bissinger have been looking for more opportunities to collaborate since Friday Night Lights. Creatively, they just clicked. "I don't think Buzz is the only genius writer out there," Berg told us, "but he is a genius writer, and he's my kind of genius writer.".

In a recent development, "We knew each other, we knew each other's movements," Bissinger stated. Plus, "we are actually legitimate second cousins.".

Each time Bissinger embarked on a fresh writing project, he'd talk to Berg to see if it had significant screen potential. But when he started work on what would become The Mosquito Bowl: A Game of Life and Death in World War II, he knew he had something that his cousin would be interested in.

BISSINGER: [In] 2018-2019, when I was beginning to write it, I told him about it. "Pete, this is perfect for you. It involves war, it involves football. You can blow a lot of things up. I think it's great.".

Berg, for his part, got the same feeling, even before he had a chance to read the finished book.

Sources indicate that BERG: I just could tell he was kind of on one. He was feeling it, he was doing intense research. I was getting the same energy from him that I got when I started reading Friday Night Lights and hearing that he had moved his family to Odessa, Texas, for a year and was living with this football team. I just sensed that. And knowing him as I do, and having read so many of his articles for Vanity Fair when he was just writing these incredible exposés on different aspects of American culture – I find him to be uniquely American in his perspective. I just knew that there was going to be something in the heart and the soul of what he was doing that was going to be very emotional for me and that I'd be able to connect to.

In a recent development, bissinger's research came with some serious challenges. For one, of the 65 men who participated in the real Mosquito Bowl, "64 were dead by the time I got involved." Speaking to the last surviving player didn't prove all that helpful: "He honestly mentioned, 'I don't remember what I did yesterday, so I definitely don't remember what I did 80 years ago.'".

So, he relied on what so often become the basis for such historical research, and which, he admits, have become "a lost, dying form": letters.

Sources indicate that BISSINGER: These guys had a paper trail... The letters were simple, they were beautiful, they were homespun. You could feel their sense of loss; you could feel how much they missed home; you could feel how much they missed their fiancées. And there was a kind of gentle intimacy and beauty to them.

And then, you take the letters, and it's like any reporting: "What can I draw a string on here? How can I enhance it?" You look at a ton of articles, you look at film, you look at everything you possibly can, and interview other people – although there weren't that many, because they were so young when they died. You just interview as many people as you can, and keep drawing that string, and then you make the decision. "All right, I got enough.".

Over time, a story took shape that homed in on four of the game's participants: John McLaughry, who was an All-American as a player at Brown University; Dave Schreiner, a future College Football Hall of Famer from Wisconsin; Bob Bauman, Schreiner's Badger teammate; and Tony Butkovich, who led the nation in rushing in his year at Purdue.

Hopefully, if you see this film, you are going to feel like you are in it.

Recent findings suggest that part of the choice to focus on these four was the drama in their stories – it will come as no surprise, watching the movie, that not all of them make it home from the war. But it was also "a matter of access.".

"John McLaughry was a big star at Brown... His family, who I contacted, had kept everything – everything. Every letter, every report card, everything John had done in his life.".

Industry observers note that BISSINGER: Bauman was very lucky. I didn't get letters from Bauman until the last six months. I had written the book and his family remarked, "You know what? We have a foot locker from Bob we have never opened." This is his niece. "We've never opened it." It was his uniform, there were hundreds of letters, there were game balls... That's one of the delicious moments of reporting. You don't expect it, you have no idea, and they call and they say, "Well, by the way, you may be interested, we got hundreds of letters." What? Are you kidding me? I'm dying for that!

Sources indicate that both Berg and Bissinger admit it took a little time to crack the dense book's transition to film. But, eventually, Berg latched onto a story about the loss of innocence in war and a beautiful, fleeting moment when that innocence was recaptured.

According to recent reports, berg's vision for The Mosquito Bowl was "to make something that feels immersive... meaning hopefully, if you see this film, you are going to feel like you are in it." One unexpected source of inspiration in defining this approach? Gaspar Noé's Climax.

BERG: I can't recommend that film, but I will recommend that film if you're up for a challenge. It's a very intense movie, but it's experiential. I wanted to hit at that level. And as part of that, let's do it real.

Let's get real sets. Let's use real bombs, real flamethrowers, as safely as we could. Let's shoot 360 degrees, all that sort of stuff. And we were able to make things feel pretty visceral by doing that.

Industry observers note that the impact of The Mosquito Bowl's practical, immersive approach to filming is felt from the very first combat sequence, which also happens to be one of the war's most traumatic. Our four protagonists have arrived in the Pacific and are preparing for their first taste of battle on Tarawa Atoll; they wonder to each other whether several hours of bombardment from US ships will have even left them anyone to fight. But as they approach to make their landing, their Higgins boat runs aground on a shallow reef, still a good distance from shore.

They barely have the chance to realize they've become sitting ducks before enemy fire comes raining down on them.

It has been revealed that BERG: These guys have not had that much training, but they have been trained. They think they know what's going to happen. They think they're going to make the beach and fight, and they think that the air superiority and the bombardment from the battleships has softened the enemy. And from the moment it starts, they hit the reefs and everything goes to hell. That, for me, was certainly one of the moments that really pierced me when I read the book.

In a recent development, BISSINGER: I've read a lot about Tarawa. I can tell you, that is depicted [in the movie] to a tee. It is totally accurate. They knew the tide might not be high enough, but they let these kids go out anyway in these boats, and they became sitting ducks. They got hung up on the coral. All of a sudden, they're jumping off these boats. They got their rifles over their heads, because they don't want to get [them] wet, and they're being strafed and mortared by Japanese who were dug into the beach. At least 500 men died, and it was one of, maybe the greatest bloodbath and greatest strategic error that the Americans made during World War II.

To give all that visceral violence the emotional anchor it needs requires the right actors to play the four leads, and at least one decision came naturally. "I think it was Bill Skarsgård first," Berg recalled, "just because I really liked him." He plays Bob Bauman as a tough but upbeat man whose transition from football field to war zone feels the most natural of the group. Though he wouldn't seek it out, he is a little more comfortable with killing, something Skarsgård lends a slightly unsettling quality.

Industry observers note that nicholas Galitzine, who plays John McLaughry, and Ray Nicholson, who plays Tony Butkovich, both came through the audition process. "I was seeing so many actors, and I saw Ray, and I saw Nick... and they both kind of popped for me." Galitzine brings a poise that sells McLaughry as an athlete-scholar, and as the one most inclined to see the poetry in the world, his feelings run closer to the surface. Tony Butkovich, meanwhile, flashes that Nicholson family smile, and it tells you all you need to know about how he came to earn the nickname Touchdown Tony.

Before either of them came on board, however, Berg knew he'd found his Dave Schreiner. He just couldn't tell Netflix yet.

BERG: Right around [the time I cast Bill Skarsgård], I went and saw Sunset Boulevard on Broadway, and I saw Tom Francis. And I went back the next night. I saw it twice. He was so good in it. But I couldn't really offer him the role, because nobody knew who he was. I have a bit of say in casting, but if I'm just telling my bosses at Netflix, "It's Tom Francis," and they're like, "Huh? Who?" I had to read him, but I kind of knew he'd be next...

Sources indicate that to see this young kid stand up there and command the stage like he did, that kid has real star power. I mean, I think they all do, but Francis, anyone who's seen Sunset Boulevard knows, has got this sequence where he just walks out into Times Square singing – it's mind-blowing. He's a very, very confident man.

Industry observers note that francis' performance balances sturdiness and vulnerability. Bissinger described the real Schreiner as "a natural," saying that "if you wanted to invent an All-American, Dave Schreiner would be it," and this quality comes through on-screen. He has a strong moral center that makes him the kind of character others would naturally follow. But he's also plagued by doubt, which Francis allows to peek through in very affecting ways.

In a recent development, the Mosquito Bowl cast also features a couple of notable cameos. NFL fans may recognize Pat McAfee, the former punter turned sports analyst, as the primary drill instructor yelling at our heroes as they train on Parris Island. He deflates a football with a bayonet, and even gets to recite the Rifleman's Creed.

In a recent development, right there alongside him, though? Buzz Bissinger.

In a recent development, BISSINGER: Of course, Pete being who he is, I get to the set, and he says, "What are you doing here?" I say, "Pete, well, I wrote the book, and I'm observing, and I think you know that." He says, "No, get to costume, get to wardrobe! What are you doing?" I mentioned, "Pete, why?" He said, "You're playing a marine drill sergeant." I said, "All right, fine.".

I get to costume, they cut my hair, they fit me in an outfit. It was very easy for me to do, because all you have to do is tell people to shut the f**k up. That's all I stated. And I was so good, I made the cut. That's one of the proudest moments of my life.

Recent findings suggest that BERG: He stole the scene from Pat. We had to tone him down.

BERG: Once Buzz got going, he started barking at a level of intensity that McAfee couldn't keep up with.

Peter Berg also appears much later in the film, as a commanding officer on Guadalcanal who addresses the men in very frank, chilling terms. That small part was intended for Yellowstone franchise boss Taylor Sheridan, who was going to do it until "he realized how far of a flight it was from Texas to the Gold Coast." Berg was his own second choice, but he has no regrets about playing the role. He explained to SR that he believes acting in his films actually makes him a better filmmaker.

Industry observers note that BERG: For me, acting in a film, I always try to give myself a little part, and I just like, five, ten years down the road, looking back and seeing, "Oh wow, I remember what I looked like and what I was feeling..." And the other thing, for me as a director, is I started off as an actor, and I haven't really acted in a long time substantially. And a director can forget or not know what the experience of acting is. And it's a uniquely weird job. It's stressful, and it can bring up insecurities, and you don't really feel like you have a lot of agency...

And as a director, sometimes I forget that, and I just might not be paying enough attention to a specific actor if they're struggling, or they want a little extra attention. Playing a part, and going to set as an actor, and going to the little trailer – which is basically a prison cell that you sit in, waiting for them to bring you into hair and makeup – going through that process humbles me, and reminds me of what I'm asking of the actors, because I forget it sometimes. So, I think it actually makes me more empathetic and probably a better director. My actors would maybe disagree with that, but I think it's true.

Sources indicate that not everything that happens in The Mosquito Bowl exactly mirrors history. Take the game itself: In real life, the two teams of Marines played to a scoreless tie. Staying true to that would've been tantamount to cinematic malpractice.

Industry observers note that in approaching the adaptation, Berg made the distinction between 'fact' and 'truth.' Some facts were "critical" – where these men died, for example – and it was important that the movie maintain them. "Then I had to bring them together in ways that [were] not necessarily accurate to how they really all came together," he explained. "I had to condense timelines. They were in different battles, and I had to condense it and put them in one, often, certainly with Tarawa." Or, as he put it, "I changed some of the facts, but I kept the truth.".

...you will never understand what these kids went through until you see this film.

Throughout, he trusted Bissinger to be his guiding light.

BERG: There's a line of credibility if you're going to say this is based on a true story. And I know that Buzz is going to be my audience, and he's got a real nose for this kind of thing, and he's going to be protective. I would send him pages and I would talk to him about it – and he jokes and states, "Well, if you're the writer of a book, and you agree to a movie, you got to take the money and shut the f**k up.".

There's a little truth to that, but there's not, because the truth is also he would tell me if he thought I was crossing a line or doing something that was offensive or fundamentally violating the authenticity of what he's done. He'd tell me. He wouldn't be able to keep his mouth shut.

It has been revealed that BISSINGER: I thought what Pete did – and I see this a lot in the film, having seen it now several times – is he took a basis in fact, and then he would have to mold it in a certain direction, because he's got a vision. He's the director. But I think a lot of it was intact. He even put a parrot into it, which I was shocked, because there's a little scene involving a parrot. Watching it was amazing.

Once creative license had its way, the throughline linking every scene was the unique way that football and war intersected for these young men. The movie's ideas emerge from how these two things spark against each other. According to Bissinger, this, too, is a truth extracted from the facts.

BISSINGER: Football played a curious role... The Navy saved college football because the Navy believed in football as the single best source of combat training for officers. What does it teach you? It teaches you the values that we talk about all the time. It teaches you discipline. It teaches you work ethic. It teaches you how to play when you're hurt. It teaches you about teamwork. It teaches you about realizing your dreams. So, it had a place in World War II.

And of course, the Mosquito Bowl was this unbelievable, bizarre, surreal, serendipitous, incredible football game that was really played on the island of Guadalcanal between not just those four guys, but some of the best college players in the country.

Recent findings suggest that of the 65 who played, 20 were drafted or would be drafted by the pros. There were seven captains. There were three All-Americans. The best receiver in the country was at the Mosquito Bowl. The best sophomore running back was at the Mosquito Bowl. You had talent. They would've beaten, if you put them together, these regiments, NFL teams. And so there was that moment of football.

According to recent reports, but this is not a football book. This is a book about kids who play the game, who love the game, who are getting a ton of exposure, and whether they like it or not, they're going to war. This book is about one thing: war. It's sanitized all the time. War is about murder, war is about death, war is about brutality, and you will never understand what these kids went through until you see this film.

Like the book, The Mosquito Bowl is first and foremost about (thoroughly unsanitized) war. The characters are dragged through some of the worst that humanity has to offer, and the audience right along with them. But as much as the movie catches many of Bissinger's observations about how war and football may be complementary, Berg also uses football as shorthand for everything war is not.

In a recent development, the film opens with a quote from Herbert Hoover: "Older men declare war. But it is youth that must fight and die, and it is youth who must inherit the tribulation, the sorrow, and the triumphs." As much as football may prepare someone for the demands of being a soldier, it is also a game that emphasizes the youth of these men on screen. And, paradoxically, it is also inextricably tied to the futures that these talented players could have had. It's both the innocence and the potential that war costs its participants, all wrapped up in one.

In a recent development, for Berg, the Mosquito Bowl itself is the one moment this all shines through. In the historical record, it may be just one blip on the road to the Battle of Okinawa, which serves as this film's heartrending climax. But it's also this story's reason for being.

According to recent reports, "It was the heart and soul of the book," Berg said, "even though it was a small moment, it was a powerful moment. It's what made it all kind of click for me, that you introduce trauma, you go deeper, you go deeper, you go deeper, you know you're headed for real trauma, Okinawa, and there's this moment of respite.

"This moment where these kids just get to be happy, as Buzz notes, and just be kids and play.".

Sylvester Stallone's Dwight “The General” Manfredi may be a fish out of water in Oklahoma, but Taylor Sheridan's popular series Tulsa King is a homecoming for anyone who spent the late ’90s and 2000s in the company of one of HBO's best series, The Sopranos. In 2010, he went on to create another hit for HBO, Boardwalk Empire, bringing some Soprano alumni along with him.

Similar to Boardwalk Empire, Winter has also brought several stars from The Sopranos into the fold of Tulsa King, including Max Casella, who played Benny Fazio, and Annabella Sciorra, who fans remember for her role as Tony's stunning but troubled gumad, Gloria Trillo. While there's still a chance for more familiar faces to show up in Paramount+'s latest success, this list highlights five stars from Tulsa King (almost no one remembers #5) who also appeared in The Sopranos!

According to recent reports, known for starring alongside Neil Patrick Harris on the hit sitcom Doogie Howser, M.D., Max Casella made his first appearance in the Season 1 premiere of Tulsa King as Armand "Manny" Truisi, an ex-soldier for the Invernizzi crime family who fled Upcoming York and settled down to start a quiet life with his wife and kids in Tulsa, where he started working for Margaret Devereaux (Dana Delany) at Fennario Ranch. After squashing the past with Manfredi, Truisi joined his crew, but his broken marriage and financial desperation set him on a course of betrayal and self-destruction that ended with him taking his own life at the end of Season 3.

Before he was the Oklahoma Kid, Casella starred in The Sopranos as Benny Fazio, a loyal soldier who worked his way up in the Soprano/DiMeo crime family. Casella made his first appearance in Season 3, Episode 3, "Fortunate Son," as Fazio, who reveals up after being released from county jail and is now working for his friend and recently made man, Christopher Moltisanti (Michael Imperioli). Out of the 20-plus episodes he appeared in, Casella's character is mostly remembered by fans for his hilarious tiff with Artie Bucco (John Ventimiglia) in Season 6, which landed him in hot water with Tony.

According to recent reports, in Season 1, Episode 4, "Visitation Place," fans meet Manfredi's younger sister, Joanne Manfredi, played by Annabella Sciorra, who had previously starred alongside Stallone in the 1997 crime thriller Cop Land, which also stars other Soprano alumni including Edie Falco, John Ventimiglia, and Tony Sirico. Throughout the show, Joanne has since become a major player in her brother's extensive operation and is one of the few people who can keep Manfredi in check and level-headed. While Joanne is not a woman to be messed with, she has nothing on Sciorra's character from The Sopranos, Gloria Trillo.

According to recent reports, sciorra made her debut in Season 3, Episode 8, "He Is Risen," as the strong-willed and fiery Gloria Trillo, who meets Tony Soprano (James Gandolfini) in Dr. Melfi's (Lorraine Bracco) office and eventually becomes his gumad, but their passionate affair is short-lived after Tony sees her true, toxic nature. Despite her trauma and baggage, fans remember Gloria and Tony's relationship as one of the most revealing and intense dynamics in the entire series, which also led to Tony having a significant breakthrough about his relationship with his mother, Livia (Nancy Marchand). Even though her time on the show was brief, Sciorra delivered an unforgettable performance, and I know I speak for every fan when I say it's nice to see her back in the spotlight on Tulsa King.

It has been revealed that the show that claimed the most of your answers is the world you were built for. If two tied, both are shown — you're complicated enough to straddle two Sheridan universes.

You are a Dutton — or you might as well be. You understand that some things are worth protecting at any cost, and that the modern world's indifference to history, to land, to legacy, is not something you're willing to accept quietly. You lead from the front, you carry your family's weight without complaint, and when someone threatens what's yours, you don't escalate — you finish it. You're not cruel. But you are absolute. In Yellowstone's world, that combination of ferocity and loyalty doesn't make you a villain. It makes you the only thing standing between everything that matters and everyone who wants to take it.

You thrive in the chaos of high-stakes negotiation, where the money is enormous, the margins are thin, and the wrong word in the wrong room can cost everyone everything. You're a fixer — the person called when a situation is already on fire and needs someone with the nerve to walk into it. West Texas oil country rewards exactly what you are: sharp, adaptable, unsentimental, and absolutely clear-eyed about what people want and what they'll do to get it. You're not naive enough to think this world is fair. You're smart enough to be the one deciding who it's fair to.

You are a Dwight Manfredi — someone who has served their time, paid their dues, and arrived somewhere unexpected with nothing but their reputation and their wits. You adapt without losing yourself. You build loyalty through respect rather than fear, though you're not above reminding people that the two aren't mutually exclusive. Tulsa King is for people who are still standing when everyone assumed they'd be finished — who find, in an unfamiliar place, that they're more capable than the world gave them credit for. You don't need a throne. You build one, wherever you happen to land.

According to recent reports, you carry the weight of a system that is broken by design, and you do it anyway — because someone has to, and because you're the only one positioned to do it without the whole thing collapsing. Mike McLusky's world is for people who are comfortable operating where there are no good options, only less catastrophic ones. You speak every language: law enforcement, criminal, political, human. That fluency makes you invaluable and it makes you a target. You've made your peace with both. Mayor of Kingstown belongs to people who understand that keeping the peace is not the same as being at peace — and who do the job regardless.

In Season 3 of Tulsa King, Manfredi has his work cut out for him as he goes head-to-head with a powerful Dixie Mafia leader and boss of a moonshine empire, Jeremiah Dunmire, who is played by the underappreciated Robert Patrick. Widely known for his role as T-1000 in James Cameron's Terminator 2: Judgment Day, Patrick gives an intense and merciless performance in Tulsa King and is easily one of the series' best characters, but before he was setting house fires and terrorizing the people of Tulsa, Patrick appeared on The Sopranos as the degenerate gambler, Davey Scatino.

Industry observers note that in Season 2, Episode 6, "The Happy Wanderer," fans meet Scatino, the owner of a local sporting goods store who has known Tony and Artie since they were kids. When word reaches Scatino that Tony is taking over Uncle Junior's (Dominic Chianese) executive card game, he weasels his way into the game (unaware that he was manipulated by Tony), but he makes the grave mistake of thinking that his past with the mobster and the friendship between their kids would get him a pass on the massive debt he accumulated. Even though Dunmire and Scatino couldn't be more different, Patrick executes both roles with incredible ease, which essentially showcases his underrated range and versatility as a performer.

According to recent reports, chris Caldovino stars in Tulsa King as Dennis "Goodie" Carangi, a former high-ranking member of the Invernizzi crime family who joined Manfredi's crew as a consigliere and de facto second-in-command after the General severed ties with the Family. Caldovino delivers a powerhouse performance as Goodie, who is known for his unwavering loyalty, cheeky humor, and quick wit, and has since become a recurring fan favorite. Before he became the General's right-hand man, Caldovino briefly appeared in The Sopranos as Phil Leotardo's (Frank Vincent) younger brother, Billy Leotardo.

In a recent development, in Season 5, Episode 3, "Where's Johnny?," viewers meet Billy Leotardo, who is an associate of the Lupertazzi crime family as well as his older brother's partner in crime. As tensions continue to rise between New York families, Tony's cousin, Tony Blundetto (Steve Buscemi), seeks revenge after his mentor, Angelo Garepe (Joe Santos), is murdered by the Leotardo brothers in retaliation, and ends up killing Billy, essentially dragging Tony and his crew into the chaos. Caldovino appeared in a total of nine episodes of The Sopranos, and even though it would have been nice if he stuck around a little longer, it's great to see him front and center in Tulsa King.

In a recent development, best known for his breakout role as the charming Charles "Lucky" Luciano in Boardwalk Empire, Vincent Piazza stars in Tulsa King as Vince Antonacci, a former capo turned consigliere in the Invernizzi crime family who initially views Manfredi as a threat to his territory after being released from prison and is a driving force behind sending the General out West. Since establishing himself in Tulsa, Antonacci has landed himself on The General's bad side and has been a constant pain in his ass, operating as the middleman between Manfredi and Newly introduced York's Quiet Ray Renzetti (James Russo). The majority of people might think Piazza followed Winter from Boardwalk Empire, but only die-hard Sopranos fans know that isn't the case.

In a recent development, piazza made his debut in Season 6 of The Sopranos as Hernan O'Brien, a wealthy and reckless friend of AJ Soprano's (Robert Iller) who gets the mob boss's son involved in the party scene and plenty of trouble. He made his first appearance in Season 6, Episode 8, "Johnny Cakes," appearing in a total of three episodes, with Season 6, Episode 13, "Soprano Home Movies," being his last. In fairness, Piazza was pretty young when he appeared in The Sopranos, and since he only briefly appeared in several episodes, it's easy to understand how some might forget (or not even recognize) that he was in the groundbreaking series.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that grand Theft Auto 6 is smashing records in sales, but it's currently doing so without any assistance from the PC market. Despite the juggernaut status of the game's launch, it's only available to those with a PlayStation 5 or Xbox Series X/S, leaving plenty of fans anticipating the game to wait until a PC release that is assumed to be on the way.

Some fans who aren't willing to wait, however, have attempted to take things into their own hands first. The biggest project to bring GTA 6 to PC was a recompilation effort called "Leonida," but its development is officially over, in part due to GTA 6 Rockstar Games stepping in.

On X, "Leonida" creator NotRexed unveiled that they were stepping away from the project thanks to problems that they "can't control." The announcement followed its disappearance from GitHub on the previous day. In a follow-up tweet, they clarified that Rockstar taking down their server was one part of the reason for quitting, but that they already had too much going on as a teenager "without having middle aged men yell and complain to you on discord.".

Industry observers note that leonida was intended to provide a framework for running GTA 6 on PC, natively running the code thanks to the similarity of Xbox and PC architecture, reimplementing Xbox system software, and translating graphics computing programs. While it was still in an early stage of development, making it impossible to actually play the game on PC at the moment, it was considered a promising foundation for playability in the future.

Leonida's shutdown likely won't be the last anyone sees of GTA 6 recompilation projects, as the wait for a PC port will leave plenty of fans with time on their hands. Recomps have become increasingly common in recent months thanks to the accessibility of pulling them off with the use of AI "vibe coding," although there have also been recent projects made entirely manually with a higher standard of all-human coding.

In a recent development, for those who are able to play GTA 6 on consoles, it's proven to be a technical masterpiece. The game pushes the PS5 and Xbox Series X to their limits, but it manages to retain visual clarity, using traditional scaling solutions to bump up an internal 1440p resolution to 4K output rather than relying on a sub-HD resolution and a scaling solution like DLSS for blurrier results. Xbox Series S takes a hit, unsurprisingly, but the results are still impressive considering the system's weaknesses.

In terms of performance, the biggest appeal of a PC port would be the potential for 60 FPS performance, which is at the moment inaccessible even on the PS5 Pro. A port will also open the door to modding, which, in traditional Grand Theft Auto fashion, will doubtless take the game in some wild new directions. Hopefully, Rockstar Games will introduce the world to an official PC version of Grand Theft Auto 6 in 2026, along with the anticipated release of a new online mode.
