  • Netflix has been arguably the biggest trailblazer for K-dramas in the streaming age, and its crown shows no indication of slipping as it approaches an ambitious December rollout.
  • Industry observers note that across the board, 2026 has been a stellar showing for Korean content, with the long-awaited release of Disney+'s The Remarried Empress recently shaking up Q4.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Shealyn Scott is a Senior Writer at Screen Rant. She has been writing for the site since 2024, focused on network, reality, streaming, and classic television. A creative writer, journalist, and lover of the written word in all its forms, Shealyn enjoys deconstructing scenes from her favorite shows, using context clues and historical precedent to predict major plot points (which, due to her successful track record, has sparked rumors of clairvoyance). As an award-winning student journalist, Shealyn spent her college years advocating for the humanities while studying English Literature. Her love of storytelling propelled her to expand her degree with minors in Writing and History, believing life to be a mere collection of stories that can be framed in as many ways as a movie scene. As a Senior member of the TV Team, Shealyn treats the series she covers like books, analyzing every line, camera angle, and lighting choice. Thankfully, her personal mission statement lines up perfectly with Screen Rant: every creative work deserves just as much thought from the viewer as it received from its creator.

Netflix has been arguably the biggest trailblazer for K-dramas in the streaming age, and its crown shows no indication of slipping as it approaches an ambitious December rollout. There have already been incredibly successful series in Netflix's 2026 K-drama lineup, ranging from the record-breaking dark comedy Teach You a Lesson to the star-studded superhero drama The Wonderfools to the action-packed return of Bloodhounds season 2— among countless other streaming hits that span every sub-genre imaginable. Of course, one impending title has lingered in the minds of K-drama fans since it was first teased at the beginning of the year: Tantara.

Industry observers note that across the board, 2026 has been a stellar showing for Korean content, with the long-awaited release of Disney+'s The Remarried Empress recently shaking up Q4. Nevertheless, Tantara has flown under the radar for many unassuming viewers. Throughout the year, flashier titles like supernatural romance Spooky in Love, murder mystery The Art of Sarah, and fantasy period drama The East Palace have captivated viewers with easily accessible, genre-focused storytelling. Comparatively, Tantara seems far more specialized, with stripped-back first looks painting a deceptively simple picture of the upcoming release. Regardless, Tantara will actually be an epic K-drama event spanning an entire month.

When Tantara was declared as part of Netflix's 2026 content plan, it may have initially appeared to be a typical period piece K-drama with a melodramatic plot and bittersweet climax. Thankfully, everything that has subsequently been released— from exciting episodic stills to a high-octane teaser trailer— has revealed the truth: Tantara will be an introspective look at the merciless Korean entertainment industry in the mid-to-late 20th century. Furthermore, it will be a slow-burning narrative that's sure to dominate Netflix's December release schedule.

It has been revealed that the musical epic will be 22 episodes total, with the first eight landing on December 11, episodes 9–15 releasing December 18, and episodes 16–22 rounding out the K-drama on December 22. While plenty of viewers will binge the drama's three distinct parts immediately, watching a single episode a day starting from the December 11 premiere would offer enough content to last you the rest of the year. As opposed to airing one or two installments a week, dropping episodes in batches will undoubtedly set Tantara up for streaming success, just like 2025 predecessor When Life Gives You Tangerines.

Industry observers note that aside from Netflix's clever release strategy, what we know about Tantara already makes it a must-watch. The K-drama will combine many of the industry's most popular current trends. For instance, period dramas that take place within the past century have seen a noticeable uptick in recent years, with 100 Days of Deception being Netflix's latest 20th century-set hit. Likewise, thematic explorations of fame and celebrity have slowly but steadily become more commonplace, with 2026 Netflix K-dramas like Can This Love Be Translated?, We Are All Trying Here, and Four Hands, Two Sonatas all touching on the dark side of stardom.

Similarly, Tantara's main cast holds significant appeal for longtime K-drama fans. While beloved female lead Song Hye-kyo (Autumn in My Heart, Encounter, The Glory) will star as Min-ja, K-drama heartthrob Gong Yoo (Coffee Prince, Goblin, Squid Game) will play romantic lead Dong-gu. Based on the synopsis and trailer, Min-ja and Dong-gu will break into the entertainment industry together, but they'll also balance a friends-to-lovers plot that First-Gen K-drama fans could only dream of. Additionally, though both actors are powerhouses on their own, Tantara marks their first on-screen collaboration, making it monumental for the K-drama genre at large.

According to recent reports, while the growing anticipation for Tantara is deserved, it could act as a double-edged sword. Surface-level aspects of the series may be enough to hook a viewer, but a 22-episode run is rare for modern K-dramas, and the extra episodes only leave more room for failure. Nevertheless, there's an inexplicable allure to the upcoming drama that has managed to assuage most fears. Only time will tell whether Tantara can stand toe-to-toe with its contemporary giants, but Netflix may have saved its best K-drama of 2026 for last— and what a gift it would be.

The first eight episodes of Tantara premiere December 11 on Netflix.

These Are the Best Early Black Friday Deals on Kindles and E-Readers

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1326 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Lifehacker

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Amazon's Black Friday sale kicked off today, which means it's a good time to score some of the year's best prices on e-readers.
  • In a recent development, because of this, the prices aren't nearly as low as they were last year, but now is still the time to get a decent discount on a Kindle Paperwhite or Colorsoft—but if you'd rather read differently, you can also save significant on a few worthy Kindle alternatives.
  • In a recent development, the Kindle Paperwhite Signature Edition is the best e-reader for most people.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Amazon's Black Friday sale kicked off today, which means it's a good time to score some of the year's best prices on e-readers. Timing your purchase is now a bigger deal than ever (so to speak), as Amazon recently raised the price of basically every Kindle by $50 or more due to the ongoing RAM crisis.

In a recent development, because of this, the prices aren't nearly as low as they were last year, but now is still the time to get a decent discount on a Kindle Paperwhite or Colorsoft—but if you'd rather read differently, you can also save significant on a few worthy Kindle alternatives. Here are your e-reader best bets in the lead-up to Black Friday and Cyber Monday.

In a recent development, the Kindle Paperwhite Signature Edition is the best e-reader for most people. An upgraded version of the basic Kindle, the Paperwhite adds a larger screen, temperature-adjustable lighting, water resistance, and better battery life—and if you opt for the Signature Edition, you also get double the storage and no lock screen ads. Earlier this year, it jumped in price to $250, even before the manufacturer introduced a latest model—but you can get the 2024 model for $179.99, 28% off the new list price.

Industry observers note that if you want a great Kindle but you don't care about paying extra for more storage or getting rid of lock screen ads, the non-Signature Edition of the Kindle Paperwhite is also a great buy right now. The 2024 model has been discounted to $129.99 from the list price of $199.99. It's available in standard black, Jade, or Raspberry colors.

Recent findings suggest that if you don't need the bells and whistles of the Paperwhite, you can also pick up the standard Kindle. It's still a very capable device, with good lighting, 16GB of onboard storage, and the ability to hook up your Bluetooth speakers to listen to Audible audiobooks. The standard Kindle, which now retails for $150, is marked down to $119.99, making it the cheapest Kindle option. Though I think it makes more sense to spend $10 more on the Signature Edition, this is the way to go if you want the cute Matcha color.

It has been revealed that if you like to read comics or you just appreciate looking at your book covers in full color, the 2024 Kindle Colorsoft is also at a strong 41% discount for Black Friday, bringing it down to around $170. For $10 less than the Paperwhite Signature edition, you get all the same perks (including an ad-free experience) and a color e-ink screen that's great for reading magazines, graphic novels, and manga. Color e-ink isn't for everyone, but if it's for you, the Colorsoft has the best color screen on the market. For an extra $10, the Colorsoft Kids Edition adds a case, a yearlong subscription to Kindle Kids+, and an extended warranty.

According to recent reports, if you're looking for a combination e-reader and e-notebook, the Kindle Scribe is a great option. With a larger screen than Amazon's other e-readers, it offers all the benefits of the Paperwhite but adds support for the excellent Premium Pen stylus, allowing you to take notes in your Amazon e-books or create handwritten documents that you can later convert to text using the onboard AI tools. The 32GB black-and-white version of the Kindle Scribe is currently $349.99, while the Colorsoft version will run you $449.99. Both of these are the newest models, released in 2025.

The newly introduced Kindle Scribe Colorsoft has all the same great features of the black-and-white version discussed above, but adds a full-color e-ink display. Combined with the large 11-inch screen, this makes it a great device for reading comics or magazine articles as they were meant to be read, or marking up PDFs using the included Premium Pen. This device usually costs a hefty $630, but the current Black Friday sale cuts $180 off of that price.

If you want to step outside of the Amazon ecosystem, the Kobo Libra Colour is a good bet. Discounted $30 to $229.99 at Best Buy, it's right now pricier than the Kindle Colorsoft, but you get a bit more for your money. While most of the specs are similar (they both use the same Kaleido 3 screen and offer 32GB of storage), the Kobo supports a stylus, so you can jot down notes in your books or keep a digital journal. It also has physical page-turn buttons, which the Colorsoft lacks.

According to recent reports, if you don't want to be tied to the Amazon ecosystem and/or you're looking for a device that's a bit more portable, consider the Viwoods AiPaper Reader, presently marked down to $200, its lowest price ever. It's got a 6.13-inch screen, so it's the same size and shape as your phone, and it has a crisp e-ink screen with a strong (if not temperature-adjustable) front light and 128GB of onboard storage. The best part is, it runs on an open Android system, so you can install multiple reading apps, including Kindle, Nook, Kobo, and Libby, and keep all of your books in one place. (Check out my review of the Viwoods AiPaper Reader for more—it's a nifty little device.).

It has been revealed that if you don't have a large Kindle library, you're moderately tech-savvy, and you praise portability above all else, I can't recommend Xteink's line of e-readers more highly. The 4.3-inch Xteink X4 Classic is at its lowest price ever, coming in at just under $55, around $34 off the list price. Meanwhile, the smaller 3.7-inch Xteink X3 is about a dollar more; that's a less-generous 19% discount. I own both, and while the Classic is definitely worth the current sale price, I actually prefer the form factor of the smaller X3 (right now $55.72), which is about the size of a library card.

For about $30 more than the X4 Classic, you can upgrade to the Xteink X4 Pro, which happens to be Lifehacker's e-reader Gift of the Year pick. It offers all the perks of the other Xteink devices, with two critical quality-of-life upgrades: A touchscreen for easier navigation, and a temperature-adjustable front light so you can read it in a dark room. (Less obviously, it also has a slightly faster processor that makes the whole thing feel a little snappier.) Right now, the X4 Pro is at its lowest price ever when ordered directly from Xteink: $84, or around 15% off the usual $99 price.

If you're feeling tentative about trusting a seemingly no-name Chinese tech brand, read more about the devices in my review, or listen to the collected wisdom of the tens of thousands of people in the bustling r/xteink Reddit group.

Recent findings suggest that in short, yes, Black Friday still offers discounts that can be rare throughout the rest of the year. If there’s something you want to buy, or you’re shopping for gifts, it’s a good time to look for discounts on what you need, especially tech sales, home improvement supplies, and fitness tech. Of course, if you need to save money, the best way to save is not to buy anything.

Follow our Black Friday coverage for the latest and best deals our team finds. Another good tip is to only buy what you need. It sounds simple, but making a list of the things you want before jumping into a sale with millions of products helps you focus and make smarter decisions.

No. If you find the product you're looking for with a major discount right now, get it. It's not likely to drop any lower, but it could always run out of stock. Take advantage of price matching or guarantees instead of waiting. Remember, you can always return products later if you change your mind. For the majority of products, the deal from Black Friday will be the same one on Cyber Monday.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Academy Award winner Kevin Kline is set to star opposite the previously announced Meryl Streep in The Corrections, Netflix‘s series adaptation of Jonathan Franzen’s National Book Award winner from Paramount Television Studios.

Recent findings suggest that kline plays Alfred Lambert, the husband of Streep’s Enid Lambert. A once-powerful patriarch battling the afflictions of aging, Alfred is a man of strict principles and old-fashioned decorum who must come to terms with his three very modern children — a daughter whose secrets he can no longer protect, an older son who has displaced him as the authority in the family, and a wayward son whose forgiveness he yearns for. Related Stories News Netflix Dates Jamie Foxx's Olympic Boxing Drama 'Fight For '84' News 'The Murder of JonBenét Ramsey': Melissa McCarthy & Clive Owen Play Grieving, Overly Scrutinized Parents In Trailer For Netflix Series.

The series brings Kline and Streep back together more than 40 years after they first collaborated on Sophie’s Choice, the Academy Award-winning classic which marked Kline’s feature film debut. Over the years, the duo have also worked together on the films A Prairie Home Companion and Ricki and the Flash, along with a handful of stage productions. Watch on Deadline.

The Corrections is a comic portrait of a Midwestern family whose three unmoored adult siblings desperately resist their mother’s wish for one last Christmas together — each undone by the delusional ambitions that were supposed to save them from becoming their parents.

Franzen adapted his book for Netflix and exec produces the limited drama alongside American Fiction‘s Cord Jefferson, who also directs all episodes. Other exec producers include Mark Roybal (Task, Mare of Easttown) and Paul Lee (Task, The Summer I Turned Pretty) for wiip; Nicole Clemens (Sexy Beast, Shantaram); Amy Sayres and Streep.

An Oscar and three-time Tony Award winner, Kline is best known for turns in such classic films as A Fish Called Wanda, Sophie’s Choice and The Substantial Chill. Most recently, he’s been seen starring in MGM+’s American Classic, opposite Laura Linney, and Alfonso Cuarón’s Emmy-nominated Apple series Disclaimer, opposite Cate Blanchett and Sacha Baron Cohen. He is repped by UTA and Berwick & Kovacik.

According to recent reports, update, November 19, 4:46 p.m. ET: The release candidates are now available to public beta testers, with the same build numbers as the developer RCs.

In addition to macOS 27.3 beta 2, Apple is also rolling out the first Release Candidates for macOS Sequoia 15.8.4 and macOS Tahoe 26.7.4. Here are the details.

Two weeks ago, Apple released macOS Tahoe 26.7.3 and Sequoia 15.8.3, along with macOS 27.2.1 Golden Gate, all of which included security fixes related to AirPlay, Bluetooth, and Messages, among others.

Today, the tech giant released the first RCs for macOS Sequoia 15.8.4 and macOS Tahoe 26.7.4, along with the second developer beta for macOS 27.3.

As is usually the case with direct-to-RC rollouts, Apple’s notes mention only that the updates provide ”security fixes for your Mac.” The actual release notes will likely become available soon after Apple officially releases macOS Sequoia 15.8.4 and macOS Tahoe 26.7.4 in the coming weeks.

The build for macOS Sequoia 15.8.4 RC 1 is 24H319, and the build for macOS Tahoe 26.7.4 RC 1 is 25G422.

According to recent reports, the Oura Ring 5 is the world’s smallest smart ring and looks more like a piece of stylish jewelry than a fitness tracker. Though it’s rarely discounted, it’s at the moment seeing a record-low price of $299 (originally $399) in this early Black Friday deal.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, bloomberg reports that Apple is hiring engineers to develop an autonomous AI agent capable of browsing the web, writing code, and controlling apps on behalf of consumers. Here are the details.

In a report published today, Bloomberg notes that upcoming job listings on Apple’s website indicate the organization’s efforts to develop an autonomous AI agent capable of performing complex tasks on the user’s behalf.

Since the breakout success of OpenClaw, autonomous AI agents have become increasingly popular, with companies such as OpenAI, Anthropic, Meta, and SpaceXSI among those offering their own solutions.

The increasing popularity of these agents has put Apple under pressure to catch up, while the tech giant has also introduced latest restrictions on how third-party AI agents can access and control Macs.

Last month, Apple announced looks to tighten macOS privacy controls around Full Disk Access, with changes introduced in the macOS 27.3 beta that give users more granular control over which apps and information third-party AI agents can access.

In a recent development, over at the App Store, Meta’s Muse has become one of the fastest-growing apps in US history, surpassing 10 million downloads in just 40 days, according to Sensor Tower, and spending weeks at the top of the charts. As of today, it sits at No. 2 among free apps, behind TikTok.

And while there are differences in how phone-based and computer-based agents operate, these systems can usually work together, coordinating tasks across devices and apps to accomplish increasingly complex goals.

Back to Bloomberg’s report, it notes Apple recently posted newly introduced job listings that offer a closer look at its intends to develop autonomous AI agents:.

It has been revealed that in one, Apple stated it’s seeking a senior engineering manager for a proactive, agentic AI assistant. The system will write code, browse the web, control apps and navigate devices on a user’s behalf, according to the post.

One job listing, which is for “Senior Engineering Manager, Agentic AI – Proactive,” features the following summary:.

“Imagine an AI agent that can use a computer the way a capable person does. It browses the web, works across apps, runs commands, writes and debugs code, and calls services, and it chooses the right tool for each step. It does all this privately and with the polish people expect from Apple. Our team is building the foundation for that future, and we’re looking for a senior engineering leader to make it real.”.

The listing also notes that Apple is building agents that can “plan and carry out multi-step tasks across apps, browsers, command lines, code, and APIs, and they can coordinate specialized sub-agents along the way,” much like existing solutions from frontier AI labs.

Today’s report on the upcoming job listings comes just days after Bloomberg reported that Apple wants to make Siri more like an autonomous AI agent, with the ability to proactively carry out tasks without requiring owners to initiate every step. According to Mark Gurman, the organization could introduce these capabilities as soon as next year.

With the new job listings, Apple has offered a more detailed look at its prepares for autonomous AI agents, although the language suggests that development is still in its early stages.

Of course, given how rapidly the technology is evolving, the landscape could look very different by the time Apple is ready to introduce its own solution next year, much like how the industry had already moved toward autonomous agents by the time Apple finally debuted its long-awaited Siri AI overhaul.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Our grandparents could drop some treats in a sock and call it Christmas, secure in the knowledge that their children would be delighted by an orange. These days, though, everyone from your tech-obsessed granny to your cutting-edge teen wants to be impressed. Luckily, there's a mind-blowing high-tech gadget out there for everyone.

Industry observers note that I don't know anyone who wouldn't appreciate finding these display glasses in their Christmas stocking. The Xbx a01s are sunglasses you can plug into any device with a USB-C port to create your own personal, private monitor. The resulting picture is the equivalent of a 142" TV. The refresh rate is a crisp 120Hz, and the glasses support HDR10 and real-time SDR-to-HDR upscaling and billions of colors, all in a package that weighs only 62 grams. In other words: It's an HD TV you can carry in your pocket and wear on your face. The $299 list price won't break your wallet either. They're the best smart glasses for most people. Check out my full review for more details.

According to recent reports, it can be hard to buy a gift for a health-focused person. They usually don't want booze and they like putting in effort. But the Whoop Peak 5 fitness tracker will brighten the Christmas morning of the most diehard athlete. It's more versatile than a watch (you can wear it on your bicep and even in your underwear) and it monitors heart rate, respiratory rate, heart rate variability, skin temperature, blood oxygen levels, daily activity, and sleep—basically everything I don't worry about. Check out Lifehacker's senior health editor Beth Skwarecki's in-depth look at the Whoop Peak 5 for more details.

You cannot go wrong with a GoPro. The tech giant's easy-to-use, hard-to-break cameras are synonymous with "action photography" and compact enough to fit in a stocking. If there's a snowboarder, skateboarder, kayaker, or BMX racer on your list, this is a must. Even if your giftee isn't an adventurer, the GoPro Hero 13 supports additional lenses and filters that let users go beyond the "gnarly fish-eye, dude" photography and videography of past generations. Check out associate tech editor Michelle Ehrhardt's GoPro Hero 13 review for more details.

According to recent reports, everyone wants their own droid. Beni from Mondo Robotics is a camera robot that takes 4K video while autonomously following its subject wherever they go. If you want to get action footage, there's no need to hassle with a tripod or another person: You can control Beni with the remote, or simply tell it to follow you. It can be set to track you from behind, from the side, or it can circle you, and you can adjust what it is doing from the app or remote on the fly, so there's no limit to the kind of elaborate shots it can pull off. Plus it's freakin' adorable. The $799 list price might be a bit steep for most gift-givers, but as far as how well it works and how much fun I've had using it, it's worth the money.

In a recent development, the R36 Max 2 retro handheld game console lets you take your gaming anywhere. It comes with over 20,000 games pre-installed, so you can play every title from classic consoles like the Atari 2600 or the PlayStation 1, as well as just about every arcade game anyone ever dropped a coin into, all for less than $100. I paid more than that in quarters just to beat Dragon's Lair!

In a recent development, I'm obsessed with the Yamaha Seqtrak. It crams a drum machine, sequencer, sampler, three separate synthesizers, and a speaker into a package small enough to put into a Christmas stocking. It's a complete mobile studio—everything you need to produce a song or beat—but it also integrates with your computer's DAW and other MIDI gear to become part of your home studio. All that for only $300!

Sources indicate that the Flipper Zero is a must-have device for the hardcore, glasses-wearing, circuit-bender type of techie. Its ability to do evil deeds like hack ATMs is greatly exaggerated, but the Flipper is still a technological Swiss Army knife that lets you read and manipulate the invisible waves around you, from radio waves to RFID, NFC, Bluetooth, and wifi signals. It's educational, fascinating, and powerful; how you use that power is your business.

In a recent development, if you're giving a gift to a would-be Antonie van Leeuwenhoek, this miniature, wireless microscope will rock their holiday. It's easy to set up, works with PCs, Android, or iOS devices, magnifies things up to 1000x, and takes 1080p pictures of your discoveries.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that after releasing developer beta 2 of macOS 27.3 earlier this week, the company is now rolling out the public beta for users looking to try the new features ahead of next month’s official release. Here’s what’s coming.

Last Monday, Apple released macOS 27.3 beta 2, with new privacy controls for Full Disk Access and automation tools, and the availability of Apple Intelligence in China.

Those came alongside several new features and tools on macOS 27.3 beta 1, including vertical tabs and adaptive dark mode in Safari, native Live Activities support, Markdown rendering in Quick Look, additional checks for potentially harmful content shared through iCloud links, and Siri AI support for Traditional Chinese, Norwegian, Turkish, and Vietnamese.

It has been revealed that and speaking of Siri AI, macOS 27.3 also expands the assistant’s capabilities across Apple’s own apps, allowing customers to perform more complex actions in Messages, Music, Calendar, Photos, and Reminders, as well as manage files and folders. Apple is also introducing latest tools for third-party developers to build more advanced Siri AI integrations using Markdown-based instructions.

While macOS 27.2 was a rather uneventful update, macOS 27.3 is shaping up to be the biggest update since the release of macOS 27, and people on the public beta can now try out these new features ahead of their official release.

The release build for macOS 27.3 public beta 2 is 26C5047e, which matches the developer build.

If you’d like to join Apple’s free public beta program, visit beta.apple.com.

Sources indicate that did you spot anything newly introduced in today’s beta? Let us know in the comments.

10 Hacks Every 'GTA 6' Player Should Know

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1250 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Lifehacker

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • I've been playing Grand Theft Auto VI since launch, and I'm having a blast so far.
  • I'm not going to share any spoilers here, but you should know that the side quests in Chapter 1 are vital.
  • If you're used to playing racing games, you'll find the driving experience in GTA VI to be quite different.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I've been playing Grand Theft Auto VI since launch, and I'm having a blast so far. The world feels even more detailed and immersive than previous GTA games, which means there's a lot to learn beyond the basic tutorials and prompts the game shares at the beginning. These are the 10 GTA 6 hacks I used to improve the game's quality of life. If you do the same, you'll spend more time immersed in the world, and less time fighting the game's default settings.

I'm not going to share any spoilers here, but you should know that the side quests in Chapter 1 are vital. If you ignore all the optional quests or small asks by other characters, you won't be able to return to those later. These are small things like fixing up the house for Lucia, meditating with her, and buying her a necklace when she asks you to. All of these have an impact on your progress. Take your time in this chapter, and remember to save before starting the mission called "Recalibration." That mission leads to Tourist Trap, which is the point of no return for Chapter 1.

If you're used to playing racing games, you'll find the driving experience in GTA VI to be quite different. It's hard to keep an eye on minimap directions while you're also getting used to vehicles in the game, and I used voice navigation to ensure that I don't keep getting lost, particularly for time-sensitive missions. You can enable this by going to GTA VI settings > Audio > GPS Voice > Voice. If you're playing the game on PS5, your DualSense controller's speaker plays GPS voice prompts. This is great as those alerts can be hard to hear over all other in-game sounds from your TV's speaker.

According to recent reports, using GTA 6's default controls, making Jason and Lucia run is quite annoying. The game makes you hold L3 to run, which hurts my thumbs. If you alter movement speed in settings, you can make the characters run just by using the left stick. You can walk by easing off the left stick, or switch to a fast walk, jog, or run when you push the stick all the way. Tweak this by going to GTA VI settings > Gameplay > Movement Speed > Jog. This lets you move faster without draining your stamina. You can also change from Jog to Run if you want the fastest possible movement speed with the left stick. Having remarked that, my pro tip is to go to Control Scheme in settings, and switch to Classic. This lets you run by holding the X button, as opposed to L3 with default controls.

Industry observers note that haptic strength is one area where GTA 6 takes the immersion a bit too far, as it's dialed up to the maximum level by default. This makes the controller's vibration strength a bit too intense for my liking, and also has a negative impact on battery life. You can fix that by reducing haptic strength a little. It's under GTA VI settings > Controller > Vibration & Haptics Strength.

Industry observers note that many modern controllers develop "stick drift," an concern where small movements of the analog sticks register as large inputs. This causes a big problem in games that require precise inputs, such as GTA 6. To counter this potential problem, the game allows you to adjust the deadzone for each analog stick in your controller. That remarked, this setting can be used to your advantage, even if you don't have stick drift issues in your controller. I recommend dialing up the deadzone to 7 to improve the driving experience. I find most cars in GTA 6 to be a bit floaty to drive, and adjusting the deadzone fixes this issue to a large extent.

Committing a heist attracts heat in GTA 6, and there are many different ways to escape the attention of in-game cops. The usual tricks include stocking up on outfits to change into, parking your vehicle a block or two away, and being so stealthy that you leave no witnesses to your crimes. However, an underrated trick involves using the pickup truck you get at the start of the game. Get a bike in the game, and stash it in your pickup truck. Then, use the truck to drive to the crime scene, and hide the truck a short distance away. Unload the bike, and use it to get to the crime scene. Once the heist is complete, ditch the bike, and run to your truck. Witnesses won't have seen you using the truck, which allows you to escape the area quickly.

Sources indicate that if you are using a car as a getaway vehicle, you can use two tricks to make a smooth escape. First, double-tap the Triangle button to exit your vehicle without switching off its engine. When you return to the vehicle in a hurry, you can escape a lot faster. If you have quick fingers, you can double-tap Triangle first, and just as your character is about to exit the vehicle, press L3 (or X, if you use classic controls). This leaves the car's door open, and saves you a little more time when you're fleeing.

Sources indicate that I suffer from chronic migraines, and I am sensitive to bright lights. Fortunately, GTA 6 has a bunch of accessibility settings that help me play the game for longer. Even if you don't face the same issues, these settings will help reduce eye strain in longer play sessions. Go to GTA VI settings > Display > Flashbang, and switch to Dark. This stops flashbangs from showing a bright white light when they go off. On the same settings page, you can tweak Player Status Effects Intensity to reduce screen effects when your character is low on health or stamina. You can also enable Brightness Reduction to reduce the intensity of bright lights in the game, and try Focus Trail Colorblind Mode if you find it hard to distinguish between different colors.

According to recent reports, I haven't been able to play first-person shooters for decades because the camera movement makes me nauseous and gives me a headache. Of late, I've noticed that it's getting harder to play third-person games too. My first two hours in GTA 6 had me quite worried because I was feeling quite sick, and I had to turn off my PS5. Luckily for me, I found a few tweaks to mitigate this problem. You can do that in GTA VI settings > UI > Persistent Center Dot. This permanently shows a white dot in the center of the screen, and it reduced my motion sickness enough to help me play the game. You can also go to GTA VI settings > Camera, reduce Camera Bob, and turn off Camera Shake, and Weapon Sway. I also recommend going to the Controller tab in settings, and tweaking all the options under Aim & Look Sensitivity until you find a comfortable level.

In a recent development, GTA 6 includes realistic ringing sounds that linger after explosions in the game. This may be fine for some people, but it can negatively affect some players' gaming sessions. Those who suffer from tinnitus or chronic migraines may not enjoy those ringing sounds, and, luckily, the game allows you to disable them. Open GTA 6's in-game settings, and enable the feature from Audio > Tinnitus Reduction.

Dots are frontier intelligence that have your back. Powered by GPT-6 Astra, they have their own cloud computer, learn from feedback over time, and can work towards your goals 24/7. This news will have you glowing from the inside.

A fresh series based on the 2006 film Aquamarine is heading to Disney Channel and Disney+, with the movie’s original stars Emma Roberts and Jake McDorman coming on board, Disney confirmed in a press release.

In addition to diving back into their roles of Claire and Raymond, Roberts and McDorman are also suiting up as executive producers on the series.

Industry observers note that the TV show will follow Kenzi Richardson’s Coral, who moves to a seaside town, according to the press release, and begins to unravel the truth about her mother’s disappearance. In a twist that’ll really have you flipping out, Cora learns her mother is a mermaid just as her own magical powers begin to surface. Briella Guiza, Theodore Dalton and Annika Reese will also star in the show.

Sources indicate that the fresh series comes 20 years after Aquamarine hit the big screen starring Roberts JoJo and Sara Paxton the titular character. In the movie, Paxton plays a mermaid who washes ashore and promises a wish to best friends Roberts and JoJo if they can help her prove true love does exist—specifically in the form of McDorman’s dreamy lifeguard—so she can avoid an arranged marriage by her merman father.

Roberts first made a splash in June, expressing how thrilled she was to be a part of Disney’s Aquamarine show.

“I’m so excited for the upcoming series,” she told People at the time. “I absolutely cannot wait.”.

“I’m so excited to bring Claire back to life as a grownup,” the 35-year-old added. “I remember when I read the pilot, I literally got choked up. I didn’t think I would have such an emotional reaction to it, but I definitely got a little teary-eyed.”.

And looking back on it now, the American Horror Story actress could hardly believe that fans are literally giving her compliments all these years later.

“There are certain projects that it just feels like lightning in a bottle,” she noted. “It feels really cool that we were all just a bunch of girls in Australia making a movie. And now it seems like it meant a lot to people, which means a lot to us.”.

While no date has been announced for the Aquamarine series just yet, keep reading to see what the cast of the original film is up to now.

Then the star of Nickelodeon's hit series Unfabulous, Roberts' turn as Clare was her first starring film role. This lead to a years-long battle as the then-18-year-old fought in court to be released from her contract. Her case with Blackground was finally settled in 2013, though Jojo later told UpRoxx, "I didn't get any money. I didn't get any damages or anything like that. After playing Aquamarine's human love interest Raymond, McDorman went on to star as Evan Chambers on ABC Family's college dramedy Greek. Then, he played Murphy Brown's adult son in CBS' shortlived revival of the iconic series, before appearing on What We Do in the Shadows, Hulu's holiday romcom Happiest Season and the critically accalimed Dopesick.

Sursok, who played popular girl Marjorie, is best known for her chilling turn as blind baddie Jenna Marshall on Freeform's Pretty Little Liars.

These days, the Australian actress isn't keeping any lifestyle secrets as she hosts the Women on Top podcast and has her own blog, Bottle and Heels, about motherhood and mental health.

She married Sean McEwen in Florence, Italy in 2011 and the couple have two daughters, Phoenix and Lennon.

EXCLUSIVE: Theatrical tech, distribution and management corp Qube Cinema has hired Imax and 20th Century Fox distribution vet Craig Dehmel as their upcoming Head of Studio Relations.

Dehmel will be based in Los Angeles for Qube Wire, which has a global content distribution service which connects with over 7,000 theaters worldwide. In his latest position, Dehmel will lead strategic customer development and strengthen senior-level relationships across Hollywood studios, independent distributors, and content owners.

Dehmel’s 35 years in the motion picture industry includes serving as Head of Global Distribution at Imax, where he led the planning, programming, and distribution of Hollywood studio, local-language, documentary, and special-content releases across more than 1,700 Imax screens worldwide. Related Stories Sports Imax To Screen Super Bowl In Deal With Disney, NFL News Imax Inks Largest UK Deal With Cinema Chain Acquired By Former Cineworld CEO Mooky Greidinger.

Recent findings suggest that prior to Imax, Dehmel spent 16 years at 20th Century Fox, where he held senior roles in sales, strategic planning, and international distribution, culminating in his appointment as EVP, InternationalDistribution. He is a member of the Academy of Motion Picture Arts & Sciences, serving in its Executive Branch, and has been a guest lecturer at the UCLA Anderson School of Management for more than two decades. Watch on Deadline.

“Qube Wire’s growth reflects the confidence that studios, distributors, and exhibitors place in our technology and services. As our global network continues to expand, strengthening our relationships with content owners and studio partners is central to our prepares,” noted Harsh Rohatgi, CEO of Qube Cinema.

In a recent development, “Craig brings an exceptional understanding of the global theatrical business and longstandingrelationships across the industry. His appointment underscores our commitment to our studio clients and will help us build on the momentum of Qube Wire, expand our engagement across the entertainment ecosystem, and create newly introduced opportunities for our wider portfolio,” he added.

Sources indicate that dehmel stated: “I’m excited to join Qube Cinema at a time of significant growth for the company and continued evolution across the theatrical distribution landscape. Qube Wire has built an impressive global network and strong relationships with studios and exhibitors. Having worked closely with these partners throughout my career, I see considerable opportunity to build on that foundation, deepen industry relationships, and help expand the reach of Qube’s technology and services. I look forward to working with the team and our partners to support the company’s continued growth.”.

Sources indicate that you can spend plenty of time getting your Mac, display, and desk just right. But what about the chair you use every day? Between typing, taking video calls, and leaning back to watch something, your position changes throughout the day. Your chair should be able to keep up.

Recent findings suggest that that’s the idea behind LiberNovo’s ergonomic chairs, which combine support that moves with you and a choice of sizes, including the Maxis range for bigger and taller consumers. For Black Friday, LiberNovo is taking up to 42% off in the U.S., with chairs starting at $609 and offers running November 19–30.

Sources indicate that adjusting a chair for your desk is one thing. Keeping that support as you change position is another. LiberNovo’s Dynamic Support System links the neck support, backrest, armrests, and seat so they move together as you recline.

Recent findings suggest that the Bionic FlexFit Backrest adds eight flexible panels that contour independently. Rather than relying on a single rigid backrest, the design lets different sections follow your back as you shift or turn. Once you’ve adjusted the chair to fit, the system is designed to maintain contact through those movements with fewer manual readjustments.

Both the Omni and Maxis families offer five recline positions: 105, 115, 125, 135, and 160 degrees. That gives you options for desk work, a more relaxed position for watching a video, and a deeper recline for a break.

It has been revealed that A higher weight limit is only part of finding a chair that fits. Taller consumers also need enough seat depth, a headrest that reaches the right spot, and armrests with room to adjust.

According to recent reports, the LiberNovo Maxis range addresses those details with a 52 cm seat depth, a wider backrest with a flared base, and an extended-travel headrest with 140 mm of vertical adjustment and 120 mm of front-to-back adjustment. Its armrests sit lower and offer a wider, longer adjustment range to accommodate larger builds.

LiberNovo recommends Maxis for users approximately 5 feet 10 inches to 6 feet 7 inches tall, with a maximum supported weight of 399 pounds. Maxis is certified to BIFMA X5.11. The seat cushion uses firmer support at the rear and a softer front edge, while a six-spring Controlled Recline System is designed to build resistance progressively as you lean back.

It has been revealed that for a shallower seat, the Omni family offers 45 cm and 48 cm configurations. Choosing between the two families starts with fit, then comes down to which features you want.

According to recent reports, there are three feature tiers in each family. Omni SE and Maxis Manual offer manually adjusted lumbar support, without a motor or battery. Both retain the flexible backrest, dynamic support, and five recline positions.

The Maxis Electric includes motorized lumbar adjustment and OmniStretch, a five-minute powered stretch sequence used in deep recline.

Omni Pro and Maxis Airflow add Active AirFlow seat ventilation. A fan draws air through the cushion to carry heat away, and an occupancy sensor pauses the fan when you stand up. These models also include a larger 3,000 mAh rechargeable battery.

LiberNovo’s warranty covers the frame and structural components for six years, and electronic components for two years.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Clashing Through the Snow director Carlson Young found it easy to relate to the film’s two main characters, Ryan Mitchell (Christopher Briney) and Hannah Hendricks (Michelle Randolph).

Recent findings suggest that the story centers the pair, two senior editors competing to oust the other from a condensed role due to impending layoffs, chasing significant book deals for the publishing organization where they work. Ryan operates off of commercial motivation and tapping into what is popular to sell books while Hannah identifies as more of a literary purist who takes big swings with the depth of books she takes on.

According to recent reports, “[The script] really spoke to me. I felt so connected to Hannah and Ryan’s literary perspectives, and it felt like an existential conversation that I have with myself, moment to moment, constantly,” Young told Deadline. “It was easy for me to access their personalities and their inner worlds. And then I just loved the classic, holiday hijinks that ensue from there, and I was up for the challenge of trying to make a great holiday rom-com.” Watch on Deadline.

The director connected the differing stances on what sells to challenges she navigates in her own job “balancing art and commerce, and what is and isn’t viable in storytelling and in the marketplace.”.

RELATED: 7 Newly introduced Christmas Movies Coming Out In 2026 From ‘Ebenezer’ To ‘Clashing Through The Snow’.

“It is true that publishing and cinemas, these are tectonically shifting industries, and trying to find yourself your voice either as a book editor or director, whatever you’re doing, it doesn’t even need to be in a creative field,” she added. “But we’re all existing in these shifting sands, and so that was my way in. That’s why I was looking at it like that.”.

In the below interview, Young unpacks specific moments like Lukas Gage’s “scene stealer” appearance, the Buc-ee’s knockoff Luc-ee’s, Ryan’s seeking advice by talking to ChatGPT and more.

Recent findings suggest that DEADLINE: I spoke with Chris and Michelle earlier, and they mentioned you gave Chris a note comparing him to Jim Carrey. Did you have any other references? Could you expand on that?

Recent findings suggest that CARLSON YOUNG: When we were rehearsing, I kept looking at him and seeing this physical comedy coming to the surface, and I was like, “This is like some Jim Carrey. I love this for you. Go off on that.” We tweaked it and trimmed it and shaped it in the edit, but he’s really funny. I hope that he does a lot more comedy.

DEADLINE: What was your role in the Luc-ee’s knockoff to Buc-ee’s?

It has been revealed that YOUNG: I don’t know what I can and can’t say about Buc-ee’s/ Luc-ee’s, but we did our best. We did our version. I’m from Texas, Buc-ee’s is a substantial part of the psychology of a Texan, and so it was really funny, and we did our own version of it.

DEADLINE: For the part where Hannah’s in the helicopter venting to the pilot and Ryan’s driving the truck talking to AI, was there ever a blueprint to have him talking to a person or was it always going to be ChatGPT?

Recent findings suggest that YOUNG: I have to say, yes, there was [a different iteration]. I personally thought that him talking to Chat was so Ryan. It made me laugh so much. And the amount of times that I’ve caught my husband… I’m like, ‘Are you asking ChatGPT a question? Like for real? Are you serious? ‘And he is serious. It just felt really modern and so of the times, and something like his character would actually do. And I like a lot the responses that Chat has for him. It just made me laugh.

Industry observers note that DEADLINE: Lukas Gage is so funny in the small role he plays. He had a similar comedic presence in People We Meet on Vacation. How did you want to incorporate him in the storyline?

YOUNG: He’s a scene-stealer. You just give him an inch, and he will create a million miles of gold. He’s a spinster. And when we Facetimed about the character, he had the funniest ideas and instincts on it, like ‘He’s like Chris Elliott in Scary Movie.” I absolutely loved that. “That’s our north star. Let’s go do that.” He’s such a breath of fresh air once they get to the Mercyville Inn, and he’s such a phenomenal human. We’ll see him in, like, 100 more movies.

In a recent development, DEADLINE: Where did you shoot? Ryan and Hannah come from LA, but they get to New York on a road trip. How did you balance the different locations?

YOUNG: We shot in Fresh York, a bit in the city, a bit upstate. We were shooting the Hudson Valley as you know Indiana and Colorado and Utah and it definitely lent itself. We were also experiencing historic winter weather in New York, like blizzards and production shut downs. Many a hurdle, and so it was truly ‘Clashing Through the Snow.’ We had a big snow budget, and we didn’t have to use it because it was just snow everywhere.

DEADLINE: Did the snow budget get redirected to other things?

Recent findings suggest that YOUNG: Absolutely, girl. Our producers would have something to say about that.

DEADLINE: My mind goes to the music, which Prime Video is always good at getting, but the Olivia Rodrigo songs specifically….

YOUNG: That’s how we got the Olivia Rodrigo song. I like that story. I think we should go with that. We saved on snow, so we got this incredible Olivia Rodrigo song.

DEADLINE: Not only “Begged” in the film but “Take Me Home (4 Christmas)” was in the trailer.

YOUNG: I love her song in the film as well. We’re super lucky to have her.

Industry observers note that DEADLINE: You’ve done Upgraded with Prime Video as well as The Last Sunrise. I know you’re not doing Upgraded 2, but is this a partnership you’re willing to continue, maybe in the form of The Last Sunrise sequel film when those books come out?

YOUNG: Absolutely, I could, definitely, and I just generally love working with this team at Amazon. So yeah, ‘til the day I die, absolutely.

WhatsApp is gradually rolling out an increase to its group chat limit, allowing up to 1,500 participants to join in, instead of the previous 1,024 cap. Here are the details.

While there are exceptions, there are generally two kinds of WhatsApp customers: those who hate group chats, and those who can’t seem to be in enough of them.

If you’re in the second category, you’re likely aware that WhatsApp has steadily increased the number of participants allowed in group chats over the years, jumping from 100 to 256 in 2016, then to 512 and, soon after, to 1,024 in 2022.

Now, as spotted by WABetaInfo, WhatsApp is once again expanding that limit, raising the maximum number of participants in a group chat to 1,500.

According to the website, the latest limit is rolling out to users on iOS and Android, though the rollout is gradual, meaning “not every account will see the higher limit immediately.”.

Industry observers note that whatsApp is automatically updating existing groups to support the new limit. This means that admins do not need to take any action to unlock the higher capacity. As soon as the upgrade becomes available to their accounts, their groups will support up to 1500 members. As a result, the update lets admins add up to 476 new members to their existing groups.

This rollout comes as WhatsApp has been working to make group chats easier to manage. Just last month, the tech giant declared four latest features, including the ability to pin messages indefinitely, share status updates within groups, filter conversations by mentions and replies, and share recent message history with new members after they join.

#85522. Andrew Ng: Unbiggen AI

📅 09 Feb 2022 • ⏱️ 14m • 📚 Deep Dive (2893 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Ieee ↗ Open Full Page

Andrew Ng: Unbiggen AI

📅 09 Feb 2022 | ⏱️ 14 min read (2893 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ieee

⏱️ ~14 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The AI pioneer states it’s time for smart-sized, “data-centric” solutions to big issues.
  • Andrew Ng was involved in the rise of massive deep learning models trained on vast amounts of data, but now he’s preaching small-data solutions.
  • Andrew Ng has serious street cred in artificial intelligence.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The AI pioneer states it’s time for smart-sized, “data-centric” solutions to big issues.

Andrew Ng was involved in the rise of massive deep learning models trained on vast amounts of data, but now he’s preaching small-data solutions.

Andrew Ng has serious street cred in artificial intelligence. He pioneered the use of graphics processing units (GPUs) to train deep learning models in the late 2000s with his students at Stanford University, cofounded Google Brain in 2011, and then served for three years as chief scientist for Baidu, where he helped build the Chinese tech giant’s AI group. So when he says he has identified the next big shift in artificial intelligence, people listen. And that’s what he told IEEE Spectrum in an exclusive Q&A.

Sources indicate that ng’s current efforts are focused on his tech giant Landing AI, which built a platform called LandingLens to help manufacturers improve visual inspection with computer vision. He has also become something of an evangelist for what he calls the data-centric AI movement, which he claims can yield “small data” solutions to significant issues in AI, including model efficiency, accuracy, and bias.

It has been revealed that the great advances in deep learning over the past decade or so have been powered by ever-bigger models crunching ever-bigger amounts of data. Some people argue that that’s an unsustainable trajectory. Do you agree that it can’t go on that way?

Andrew Ng: This is a big question. We’ve seen foundation models in NLP [natural language processing]. I’m excited about NLP models getting even bigger, and also about the potential of building foundation models in computer vision. I think there’s lots of signal to still be exploited in video: We have not been able to build foundation models yet for video because of compute bandwidth and the cost of processing video, as opposed to tokenized text. So I think that this engine of scaling up deep learning algorithms, which has been running for something like 15 years now, still has steam in it. Having noted that, it only applies to certain problems, and there’s a set of other problems that need small data solutions.

When you say you want a foundation model for computer vision, what do you mean by that?

Ng: This is a term coined by Percy Liang and some of my friends at Stanford to refer to very large models, trained on very large data sets, that can be tuned for specific applications. For example, GPT-3 is an example of a foundation model [for NLP]. Foundation models offer a lot of promise as a fresh paradigm in developing machine learning applications, but also challenges in terms of making sure that they’re reasonably fair and free from bias, especially if many of us will be building on top of them.

What needs to happen for someone to build a foundation model for video?

Sources indicate that ng: I think there is a scalability problem. The compute power needed to process the large volume of images for video is significant, and I think that’s why foundation models have arisen first in NLP. Many researchers are working on this, and I think we’re seeing early signs of such models being developed in computer vision. But I’m confident that if a semiconductor maker gave us 10 times more processor power, we could easily find 10 times more video to build such models for vision.

It has been revealed that having mentioned that, a lot of what’s happened over the past decade is that deep learning has happened in consumer-facing companies that have large user bases, sometimes billions of people, and therefore very large data sets. While that paradigm of machine learning has driven a lot of economic value in consumer software, I find that that recipe of scale doesn’t work for other industries.

It’s funny to hear you say that, because your early work was at a consumer-facing manufacturer with millions of users.

Sources indicate that ng: Over a decade ago, when I proposed starting the Google Brain project to use Google’s compute infrastructure to build very large neural networks, it was a controversial step. One very senior person pulled me aside and warned me that starting Google Brain would be bad for my career. I think he felt that the action couldn’t just be in scaling up, and that I should instead focus on architecture innovation.

“In many industries where giant data sets simply don’t exist, I think the focus has to shift from massive data to good data. Having 50 thoughtfully engineered examples can be sufficient to explain to the neural network what you want it to learn.” —Andrew Ng, CEO & Founder, Landing AI.

I remember when my students and I published the first NeurIPS workshop paper advocating using CUDA, a platform for processing on GPUs, for deep learning—a different senior person in AI sat me down and mentioned, “CUDA is really complicated to program. As a programming paradigm, this seems like too much work.” I did manage to convince him; the other person I did not convince.

I expect they’re both convinced now.

It has been revealed that over the past year as I’ve been speaking to people about the data-centric AI movement, I’ve been getting flashbacks to when I was speaking to people about deep learning and scalability 10 or 15 years ago. In the past year, I’ve been getting the same mix of “there’s nothing new here” and “this seems like the wrong direction.”.

How do you define data-centric AI, and why do you consider it a movement?

It has been revealed that ng: Data-centric AI is the discipline of systematically engineering the data needed to successfully build an AI system. For an AI system, you have to implement some algorithm, say a neural network, in code and then train it on your data set. The dominant paradigm over the last decade was to download the data set while you focus on improving the code. Thanks to that paradigm, over the last decade deep learning networks have improved significantly, to the point where for a lot of applications the code—the neural network architecture—is basically a solved problem. So for many practical applications, it’s now more productive to hold the neural network architecture fixed, and instead find ways to improve the data.

When I started speaking about this, there were many practitioners who, completely appropriately, raised their hands and stated, “Yes, we’ve been doing this for 20 years.” This is the time to take the things that some individuals have been doing intuitively and make it a systematic engineering discipline.

The data-centric AI movement is much bigger than one company or group of researchers. My collaborators and I organized a data-centric AI workshop at NeurIPS, and I was really delighted at the number of authors and presenters that highlighted up.

You often talk about companies or institutions that have only a small amount of data to work with. How can data-centric AI help them?

Industry observers note that ng: You hear a lot about vision systems built with millions of images—I once built a face recognition system using 350 million images. Architectures built for hundreds of millions of images don’t work with only 50 images. But it turns out, if you have 50 really good examples, you can build something valuable, like a defect-inspection system. In many industries where giant data sets simply don’t exist, I think the focus has to shift from big data to good data. Having 50 thoughtfully engineered examples can be sufficient to explain to the neural network what you want it to learn.

When you talk about training a model with just 50 images, does that really mean you’re taking an existing model that was trained on a very large data set and fine-tuning it? Or do you mean a brand fresh model that’s designed to learn only from that small data set?

Sources indicate that ng: Let me describe what Landing AI does. When doing visual inspection for manufacturers, we often use our own flavor of RetinaNet. It is a pretrained model. Having said that, the pretraining is a small piece of the puzzle. What’s a bigger piece of the puzzle is providing tools that enable the manufacturer to pick the right set of images [to use for fine-tuning] and label them in a consistent way. There’s a very practical problem we’ve seen spanning vision, NLP, and speech, where even human annotators don’t agree on the appropriate label. For big data applications, the common response has been: If the data is noisy, let’s just get a lot of data and the algorithm will average over it. But if you can develop tools that flag where the data’s inconsistent and give you a very targeted way to improve the consistency of the data, that turns out to be a more efficient way to get a high-performing system.

“Collecting more data often helps, but if you try to collect more data for everything, that can be a very expensive activity.” —Andrew Ng.

According to recent reports, for example, if you have 10,000 images where 30 images are of one class, and those 30 images are labeled inconsistently, one of the things we do is build tools to draw your attention to the subset of data that’s inconsistent. So you can very swiftly relabel those images to be more consistent, and this leads to improvement in performance.

Could this focus on high-quality data help with bias in data sets? If you’re able to curate the data more before training?

In a recent development, ng: Very much so. Many researchers have pointed out that biased data is one factor among many leading to biased systems. There have been many thoughtful efforts to engineer the data. At the NeurIPS workshop, Olga Russakovsky gave a really nice talk on this. At the main NeurIPS conference, I also really enjoyed Mary Gray’s presentation, which touched on how data-centric AI is one piece of the solution, but not the entire solution. Upcoming tools like Datasheets for Datasets also seem like an crucial piece of the puzzle.

One of the powerful tools that data-centric AI gives us is the ability to engineer a subset of the data. Imagine training a machine-learning system and finding that its performance is okay for most of the data set, but its performance is biased for just a subset of the data. If you try to change the whole neural network architecture to improve the performance on just that subset, it’s quite difficult. But if you can engineer a subset of the data you can address the problem in a much more targeted way.

When you talk about engineering the data, what do you mean exactly?

Ng: In AI, data cleaning is key, but the way the data has been cleaned has often been in very manual ways. In computer vision, someone may visualize images through a Jupyter notebook and maybe spot the problem, and maybe fix it. But I’m excited about tools that allow you to have a very large data set, tools that draw your attention quickly and efficiently to the subset of data where, say, the labels are noisy. Or to quickly bring your attention to the one class among 100 classes where it would benefit you to collect more data. Collecting more data often helps, but if you try to collect more data for everything, that can be a very expensive activity.

It has been revealed that for example, I once figured out that a speech-recognition system was performing poorly when there was car noise in the background. Knowing that allowed me to collect more data with car noise in the background, rather than trying to collect more data for everything, which would have been expensive and slow.

What about using synthetic data, is that often a good solution?

Ng: I think synthetic data is an crucial tool in the tool chest of data-centric AI. At the NeurIPS workshop, Anima Anandkumar gave a great talk that touched on synthetic data. I think there are important uses of synthetic data that go beyond just being a preprocessing step for increasing the data set for a learning algorithm. I’d love to see more tools to let developers use synthetic data generation as part of the closed loop of iterative machine learning development.

Do you mean that synthetic data would allow you to try the model on more data sets?

Ng: Not really. Here’s an example. Let’s say you’re trying to detect defects in a smartphone casing. There are many different types of defects on smartphones. It could be a scratch, a dent, pit marks, discoloration of the material, other types of blemishes. If you train the model and then find through error analysis that it’s doing well overall but it’s performing poorly on pit marks, then synthetic data generation allows you to address the problem in a more targeted way. You could generate more data just for the pit-mark category.

“In the consumer software Internet, we could train a handful of machine-learning models to serve a billion consumers. In manufacturing, you might have 10,000 manufacturers building 10,000 custom AI models.” —Andrew Ng.

According to recent reports, synthetic data generation is a very powerful tool, but there are many simpler tools that I will often try first. Such as data augmentation, improving labeling consistency, or just asking a factory to collect more data.

In a recent development, to make these issues more concrete, can you walk me through an example? When a firm approaches Landing AI and claims it has a problem with visual inspection, how do you onboard them and work toward deployment?

Ng: When a customer approaches us we usually have a conversation about their inspection problem and look at a few images to verify that the problem is feasible with computer vision. Assuming it is, we ask them to upload the data to the LandingLens platform. We often advise them on the methodology of data-centric AI and help them label the data.

Recent findings suggest that one of the foci of Landing AI is to empower manufacturing companies to do the machine learning work themselves. A lot of our work is making sure the software is fast and easy to use. Through the iterative process of machine learning development, we advise customers on things like how to train models on the platform, when and how to improve the labeling of data so the performance of the model improves. Our training and software supports them all the way through deploying the trained model to an edge device in the factory.

According to recent reports, how do you deal with changing needs? If products change or lighting conditions change in the factory, can the model keep up?

Sources indicate that ng: It varies by manufacturer. There is data drift in many contexts. But there are some manufacturers that have been running the same manufacturing line for 20 years now with few changes, so they don’t expect changes in the next five years. Those stable environments make things easier. For other manufacturers, we provide tools to flag when there’s a significant data-drift issue. I find it really key to empower manufacturing customers to correct data, retrain, and revision the model. Because if something changes and it’s 3 a.m. in the United States, I want them to be able to adapt their learning algorithm right away to maintain operations.

Recent findings suggest that in the consumer software Internet, we could train a handful of machine-learning models to serve a billion users. In manufacturing, you might have 10,000 manufacturers building 10,000 custom AI models. The challenge is, how do you do that without Landing AI having to hire 10,000 machine learning specialists?

So you’re saying that to make it scale, you have to empower customers to do a lot of the training and other work.

According to recent reports, ng: Yes, exactly! This is an industry-wide problem in AI, not just in manufacturing. Look at health care. Every hospital has its own slightly different format for electronic health records. How can every hospital train its own custom AI model? Expecting every hospital’s IT personnel to invent upcoming neural-network architectures is unrealistic. The only way out of this dilemma is to build tools that empower the customers to build their own models by giving them tools to engineer the data and express their domain knowledge. That’s what Landing AI is executing in computer vision, and the field of AI needs other teams to execute this in other domains.

Is there anything else you think it’s crucial for people to understand about the work you’re doing or the data-centric AI movement?

Industry observers note that ng: In the last decade, the biggest shift in AI was a shift to deep learning. I think it’s quite possible that in this decade the biggest shift will be to data-centric AI. With the maturity of today’s neural network architectures, I think for a lot of the practical applications the bottleneck will be whether we can efficiently get the data we need to develop systems that work well. The data-centric AI movement has tremendous energy and momentum across the whole community. I hope more researchers and developers will jump in and work on it.

This article appears in the April 2022 print matter as “Andrew Ng, AI Minimalist.”.

Latest Update: Why Black Friday Is the Perfect Time to Start a Gym Membership

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (761 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Lifehacker

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Most people are probably waiting until Jan.
  • The week of Black Friday can deliver you a good discount on a gym membership, an empty gym, and a built-in two-month runway to turn a generic resolution into a real habit.
  • This week is as good a time to save of a gym membership as a newly introduced air fryer.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Most people are probably waiting until Jan. 1 to start getting in shape, whether they want to start fresh or absolve themselves of their perceived holiday indulgences. Every year, people start the new year by joining a gym crowded with others newly resolved to get in shape, paying full price for the privilege of waiting in a long line to use the squat rack. This year, try something different: Start your gym membership during Black Friday.

The week of Black Friday can deliver you a good discount on a gym membership, an empty gym, and a built-in two-month runway to turn a generic resolution into a real habit. While you're comparing deals on upcoming tech, headphones, or smart home devices, here’s why you should also take a few minutes to scout out the gyms near you.

This week is as good a time to save of a gym membership as a newly introduced air fryer. Here are just a few examples of the offers out there right now:.

Orangetheory and F45 have various free-month and prize-entry promotions for new Black Friday sign-ups, and similar studios for Pilates, yoga, and strength training have discounted multi-month and annual packages.

Independent gyms, university rec centers, and local studios often run their own versions, from a free month tacked onto a longer commitment to waived joining fees.

In a recent development, deals vary a lot by location, so call or stop by the clubs near you and ask what's available. Then remember to always read the fine print before you sign:.

Look at the price after the promotion ends, not just the first month's rate.

Ask about fees, including joining, annual, and access fees.

Try before you buy. Many gyms offer a free trial pass. It might make sense to first visit at the time of day you'd actually go.

Sources indicate that be honest about distance. The best gym is the one you'll actually walk into, so pick one that's close to home or work.

Gyms also run sales around New Year's, so a good Black Friday offer isn't the only deal you'll see. Even still, the savings aren't the only reason to go now.

December is reliably the quietest stretch of the gym year: People are busy with holiday travel and work deadlines, and many tell themselves they'll "start fresh in January." That means open benches, free treadmills, and staff who have time to show you how a machine works.

Sources indicate that that's a gift for any gym-goer, but especially if you're latest. Learning your way around a gym is much less intimidating when it's empty. You can figure out the equipment, make your mistakes in peace, and build a routine before the January crowds arrive. Plus, this time of year is a perfect window to set and achieve a winnable goal.

According to recent reports, from Black Friday to Fresh Year's Day is about five weeks. By the time the January rush hits its peak and settles into its usual patterns, you could be eight weeks into a new routine. And as my colleague Beth Skwarecki explains, you really can get a lot stronger in 24 workouts. Beginners tend to see the fastest gains of their lifting lives in the first couple of months.

Prefer running? I know I do, and luckily, a couch-to-5K plan works the same way. Most programs run about nine weeks and build you up gradually from short run-walk intervals. Start the week after Black Friday and you'll be running for a solid stretch by early January, and you'll be well on your way to 30 minutes at a stretch by the end of the month. By the time your Latest Year's resolution friends are just starting, you'll already be a few runs in.

This is also the season when many workplaces and health plans wrap up their open enrollment periods, which makes it a smart time to check what wellness perks you already have. Before you pay full price for anything, look into:.

Workplace wellness programs, which sometimes offer gym reimbursements, discounted memberships or fitness stipends.

Health insurance perks, since some plans include gym memberships or discounts.

HSA and FSA rules, where general gym memberships usually don't qualify, but some medically recommended programs may. Also check any year-end deadlines for money you'd otherwise lose.

Corporate and employer discounts, which many large gyms offer on top of regular promotions.

Stack a workplace benefit on top of a holiday sale, and your cost per workout can drop considerably—well before Latest Year's resolution time arrives.
