Recent findings suggest that about Apple @ Work: Bradley Chambers has been an Apple IT admin since 2009. Through his experience deploying and managing firewalls, switches, a mobile device management system, enterprise grade WiFi, 1000s of Macs, and 1000s of iPads, Bradley will highlight ways in which Apple IT managers deploy Apple devices, build networks to support them, train people, share stories from the trenches of IT management, and ways Apple could improve its products for IT departments.

Device management is built around the software IT deploys. Apps from Apple Business Manager, apps preloaded via your device management vendors’ packages, packages you upload, and profiles you push out. That model solves the problem for native macOS apps. It doesn’t cover what happens when the Mac becomes the default developer machine. Developers install what they need with a single command in Terminal, and Homebrew alone has more than 16,000 packages. You then add millions of npm packages and hundreds of thousands of IDE extensions, and the list of software on a Mac that IT didn’t put there is longer than the list it did.

Recent findings suggest that that used to be a developer-only problem. It isn’t anymore, in the vibe-coding era. AI tools have turned marketers, analysts, and ops people into builders, and those builders install packages too.

Workbrew started as a management layer for Homebrew: an agent that reports what’s installed, flags known vulnerabilities, and lets IT push updates across the fleet. Version 2.0 expands the catalog to include npm packages, VS Code extensions, and macOS apps, all in a single inventory. The manufacturer says it has patched more than 10 million vulnerabilities for customers since its launch, and it’s now ISO 27001-certified.

The part that is critical for everyone who isn’t a developer is the latest Workbrew app, a native Mac app for finding, installing, and updating approved software. Workbrew calls it “the app store for your entire company.” Employees can browse what IT has approved, install it without opening Terminal, and request anything that isn’t on the list. IT approves or denies in the Workbrew Console, and if it’s a no, the employee gets an answer on why.

Recent findings suggest that the app comes from the Updatest team, which Workbrew acquired as part of this release. Updatest is the indie Mac app that keeps thousands of consumers’ software up to date, and it remains a separate product for individuals and families. For business customer, that experience is now the Workbrew app, and it’s included on every initiative, including the free Team plan with no device or user limits.

With Workbrew, we finally have real visibility into what developers are using in Homebrew. Fleet-wide updates are effortless, and the team stays secure without being slowed down.

Chris Merrell, Director of IT, End User Services, Camping World.

Workbrew isn’t a device management tool and isn’t trying to be one. Your device management system deploys the Workbrew agent, and Workbrew handles software your device management system lacks visibility into. If your fleet consists entirely of office workers on managed apps, there’s nothing here for you. If you have developers, or you’ve noticed the marketing team installing things to run AI scripts, you have the problem whether you’ve discovered it or not.

Recent findings suggest that ice storms cause long outages because several exposures act together. Ice adds weight to conductors, hardware and structures. Wind pushes on the larger iced surface. Trees and limbs bend into the line and add impact and uneven load. Conductors may also gallop and lose clearance. This paper explains how these loads combine and why the complete line must be assessed, not a single component. It reviews a monitored winter test of three conductor systems. It also summarizes utility records from a major regional ice storm. Finally, it outlines how to choose corridors, proposal restoration and keep crews and the public safe around covered conductors.

Chelsea’s feisty friendly ends in penalty shoot-out confusion

📅 09 Aug 2026 | ⏱️ 16 min read (3129 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Co

⏱️ ~16 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Chelsea’s Far East tour ended in farce and confusion with players waiting around for a penalty shoot-out that never happened.
  • The chaos came at the end of a hard-earned, bad-tempered draw against Malaysian champions Johor Darul Ta’zim, with an own-goal in the 89th minute sparring the west London side’s blushes.
  • Industry observers note that that goal also was supposed to set up penalties.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Chelsea’s Far East tour ended in farce and confusion with players waiting around for a penalty shoot-out that never happened.

The chaos came at the end of a hard-earned, bad-tempered draw against Malaysian champions Johor Darul Ta’zim, with an own-goal in the 89th minute sparring the west London side’s blushes.

Industry observers note that that goal also was supposed to set up penalties. But after minutes of waiting around – and Kevin Campello, Chelsea’s head of first-team operations, saying “it’s written in the contract” – the players walked off the pitch.

According to recent reports, that confusion ended a feisty affair in which tensions threatened to boil over and that, at certain points, paid little attention to the “friendly” aspect of the clash with seven yellow cards shown. At one point the visitors’ fresh set-piece coach Austin MacPhee exchanged angry words with some of Johor’s coaching staff. The CFC TV commentary team suggested that the spot-kicks were abandoned because of the match’s heated atmosphere.

Austin MacPhee was ready to throw hands😂 pic.twitter.com/CFDgTOwmxE.

Having played just 24 hours earlier in Jakarta – a 3-0 win over AC Milan – it was no surprise to see Xabi Alonso name a fresh XI, a mixture of players who may well be offloaded before the end of the transfer window, those needing to prove themselves, and youngsters given much-needed game time.

And considering Johor are one game away from setting a upcoming world record of 109 matches unbeaten in the top flight – a run that would surpass the current mark set by Ivorian side Asec Mimosas in the early 1990s – it was also no shock to see the Malaysian team offer a stern, pre-season test for the west Londoners.

Industry observers note that after a good start Chelsea were second best in a first half in which Johor should have been at least two goals to the good. The Malaysian champions controlled the first 45 minutes and were 1-0 up after 14 minutes – a low cross from the left side-footed home by Arif Aiman.

The hosts gave the young, inexperienced Chelsea backline a torrid time, especially on the flanks and Óscar Arribas was guilty of not capitalising on a great chance to double Johor’s lead, his shot after cutting in from the right going wide.

Sources indicate that while they looked vulnerable at the back, Chelsea also struggled to keep possession in attack. But they got an equaliser they scarcely deserved after Liam Delap was manhandled to the ground in the box by Kevin Medina. The striker, who may well leave Stamford Bridge before the transfer window slams shut, fired home the spot-kick allowing the visitors to go into the break on level terms.

For the most part, the second half followed a similar pattern to the first – Jofor having the better chances, while tensions on the pitch continued to run high.

It was, however, Chelsea who took the lead after the break, Delap once again scoring from the spot, this time after Jamie Gittens was brought down in the area.

Johor, though, kept on creating, thanks in part to a fairly porous visitors’ backline, and levelled through a deflected Arribas free kick, before going 3-2 up thanks thanks to a well-taken Bérgson strike.

Had it stayed that way Chelsea could have had few complaints. But as the clock approached 90 minutes, the visitors had one last attack. Mykhailo Mudryk, just on as a substitute, delivered a cross from the left that Antonio Glauder could only steer into his own net. That was supposed to set up the penalty shoot-out that did not take place and the chance for one of the sides to claim a hollow victory.

Considering a raft of changes and that fact this was far from the first XI, it is hard to know what to make of this. But among the positive things Alonso could take from the game was the impressive form of Nicolas Jackson and good centre-forward play of Delap. The negative was, however, a poor defensive display.

Chelsea return to Stamford Bridge on Saturday for their last pre-season friendly, against Real Sociedad, before the Premier League season starts away at local rivals Fulham on August 24.

Substitutes: Curd, Diakite, Kavuma-McQueen, Sarr, Walsh.Booked: Estêvão, Delap, Jackson, Geovany Quenda, Watson.Goals: Delap (42 pen, 62 pen), Antonio Glauder (89 og).

A mixture of players who may well be offloaded before the end of the transfer window, those needing to prove themselves, and youngsters you may not have heard of.

Johor Darul Ta’Zim – more commonly known as JDT – are the Man Utd of Malaysia (at least that’s according to a Malaysian friend of mine). In 2013, they were going nowhere and were the dictionary definition of a stagnant club, low on confidence and trophies. That was until the Crown Prince bought the club and, over the next 13 years, transformed it into the powerhouse it is today.

As if to underline JDT’s dominance over Malaysian football they are one game away from the world record unbeaten run in a top flight. The newly introduced season of the Malaysian Super League gets under way later this month and should they avoid defeat in their opening match they will extend their unbeaten run - which began in April 2021 - to 109 games and surpass the world record set by Ivorian side Asec Mimosas in the early 1990s.

Recent findings suggest that chelsea’s pre-season tour of South East Asia ends today with a match against Johor Darul Ta’zim in Malaysia. The clash comes barely 24 hours after the west Londoners beat AC Milan 3-0 in Jakarta, a much-needed win coming on the back of defeats against Juventus and Tottenham.

A fine volley from Moises Caicedo and a double from João Pedro either side of half-time led Xabi Alonso’s side to victory in the Indonesian capital.

The game was fairly even in the first half and looked set to head into the break level at 0-0 but Pedro’s header from Caicedo’s corner put Chelsea in front.

Alonso’s side then doubled their advantage seconds into the second half as Pedro scored his second, assisted by Pedro Neto.

According to recent reports, just minutes later, Chelsea had their third courtesy of a well-worked corner routine. Romeo Lavia’s delivery was met by Caicedo on the volley, with the Ecuadorian’s finish with the outside of the boot finding the bottom corner.

Today, the west London side face Malaysian powerhouses Johor at the Sultan Ibrahim Stadium, more on them later, but considering the tight turnaround from yesterday’s match today’s clash will provide a stern test.

“The idea, with the game against Milan and then one in Johor, was to arrive at this weekend with players not being ready for 90 minutes until now,” Alonso explained after the win in Jakarta.

“We wanted to have a logical progression in their loads; so we had our plan and we’ve stuck to that.

“We have another idea [against Johor]; that was decided yesterday [Friday]. The idea is that many young players were coming to have chances to play tomorrow. If not, we’d have been short, as playing two games in two days is quite intense. So we will need them.”.

Stay here for all the team news and action with kick-off set for 1pm.

#85420. The new set of problems for engineers to solve

📅 25 Oct 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1101 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Katelynlesse ↗ Open Full Page

The new set of problems for engineers to solve

📅 25 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1101 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Katelynlesse

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that A lot of software engineers are going through what can only be described as an identity crisis.
  • It has been revealed that agents started out as basic, human in the loop chats.
  • Now, some folks are starting to build truly amazing multiagent systems to tackle the world's hardest and most crucial problems, like serious research, discovery, and hardware design.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that A lot of software engineers are going through what can only be described as an identity crisis. The job has changed a lot. Some are depressed, others are having the time of their lives. There's a really specific thing I see happening that makes me really excited for what engineering looks like over the next, call it a year or two - AI just isn't going to be able to create the incredible outcomes it's capable of creating unless software engineers solve problems to make it possible. This is existential, which is honestly a lot of fun, so it's a pretty incredible time to be a software engineer.

It has been revealed that agents started out as basic, human in the loop chats. Then models got better at running for longer on harder problems, and agentic systems started moving to the cloud. While that was happening, models have started to get better at working together, and people have built basic multiagent systems. Like an orchestrator that spawns some subagents for a given task, or giving agents jobs other than executing to improve outcomes, like grading or advising or dreaming.

Now, some folks are starting to build truly amazing multiagent systems to tackle the world's hardest and most crucial problems, like serious research, discovery, and hardware design. Picture thousands of agents, persistently working towards these outcomes. This comes with a latest set of software engineering problems that we're already seeing crop up.

It has been revealed that infrastructure needs to evolve to handle burstier workloads. We need proper authentication and authorization to identify agents, let them work together, enable them to take the actions they should, and prevent them from taking the actions they shouldn't. Security and proper isolation are critical for untrusted code and content. And we've gotta have monitoring and the ability to stop a system in its tracks when it's veering into the wrong territory.

Sources indicate that models will keep getting better, and these types of multiagent systems will become really powerful. But software engineers have to solve all these problems if we're going to actually unlock that power and enable the world to trust it to create good outcomes like cured diseases rather than bad outcomes.

Sources indicate that the software industry has been building on Kubernetes, which was designed for stateless, replicated apps or stable numbered sets of stateful pods. Agents are totally different. They're essentially isolated, stateful, single-instance workloads. They can go idle for arbitrary amounts of time between bits of work, and they spend a lot of time waiting on tools, model inference, other agents, or human input. Some workloads need fast startup times, others need to avoid wasting compute, and others need crazy scale. Amazing engineers are pushing hard on this problem space - like AI infra companies building new filesystems and sandboxing offerings, and the Google team building Agent Substrate as a new runtime. There's a ton left to figure out.

Industry observers note that there are problems to solve in agent authentication - identifying an agent that took an action. This area has the benefit of the building blocks that have been built and hardened from the microservices world, like workload identity with short-lived certs rather than static keys, and folks are beginning to apply these concepts to agents.

Sources indicate that agent authorization as a problem space is much more wide open - what do you allow an agent to do? Many agents work on behalf of a human, and use that human's identity and credentials to access various systems and take actions. There's already a problem in there, which is identifying that it was the agent and not the actual human who took an action. But there are deeper problems in this on-behalf-of (OBO) setup, like consent. If multiagent systems are working for weeks, how does the human meaningfully approve what their agent can do? Agentic platform features like auto approval for tool calls helps, but there's deeper permissioning needed to get this right at high scale. And then we have agents working with their own identity, which is even less solved, and how we apply that to agents working together - how does an agent trust another agent that asked it for something?

Industry observers note that over the past few months and especially in the past couple weeks, we've seen vulnerabilities surfacing faster than the industry can patch them, much of it in critical core software that many systems rely on. Now think about thousands of persistent agents running on top of that core software, writing untrusted code and reading untrusted content. Those unpatched vulns get a lot more dangerous in that world, and one of the most key things for software engineers to do is get creative about how to harden that software - kernels, browsers, runtimes, and common libraries.

According to recent reports, multiagent systems add another twist. A compromised agent could pass injected instructions to other agents it's working with, and those instructions could end up in memory for future agents to accidentally trust. Blast radius gets real - how much of the multiagent system is at risk when that first agent got compromised? Isolation becomes key in that world - agents should use strongly isolated sandboxed execution environments to take actions. I wrote a bit about that here.

Industry observers note that lastly, we need the tools to make sure these multiagent systems are working in a positive direction, and that we catch them and cut them off if they're not. We need OTel tracing across agents, and to ensure that an agent can never modify its own trace or another agent's trace. We need kill switches that monitoring can trigger, that truly stop the whole system at once and cut off its creds. Really the hard part is how to know when the system is going in the wrong direction. Well-intentioned persistence to solve a problem can look a lot like maliciousness - repeated attempts to reach a domain that isn't on its allowlist, for example.

It has been revealed that this is for the engineers feeling an identity crisis because they think their knowledge and skills won't be important - you and your skills can be the difference in whether or not these problems get tackled and multiagent systems can solve the world's hardest problems. You can and should go deep in these domains, learn latest things, and form opinions. So much of this problem space is wide open for new solutions. It's an incredibly exciting time to put your skills to work.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that for most people, dictation is far easier and quicker than typing, which raises the question: why do we still spend so much time typing out emails and documents? Often, it's because opening and setting up dictation software takes too long when you just need to get a note down quickly. SecondBrain’s VoicePad promises to be something quite different: An AI-powered dictation device that works even when you whisper, and gives you one-touch buttons for quick app launching.

It’s the ultimate desk companion.

The SecondBrain VoicePad is a CNC-machined, small, lightweight handheld device with five individual customizable buttons and dual microphones that can pick up your voice in loud environments or when you’re whispering. It’s highly portable, so you can carry it around with you for easy access to your most key apps, and to take notes and dictation whenever you need it, without all the usual “ums” and false-starts that make dictated notes so hard to read.

Workers brainstorming on a commute can take down a few key notes, or have the device’s AI whip them up into a first-draft report. Remote creators can easily record some ideas for their novel, Dungeons and Dragons campaign, or their next musical composition. Software developers who just had a flash of inspiration can flesh out the idea by triggering the VoicePad’s AI to expand on their original thought.

You can use the VoicePad for longer-form content, too, and replace the need to type almost entirely. Dictate emails, chapters of your book, or wholesale reports. With SecondBrain VoicePad, anyone can dictate at up to 160 words per minute, making it one of the fastest ways to record information accurately and effectively.

It works in any app with a text input box, too, so whatever you’re doing with words, the VoicePad can help you get them down clearly for later reading, or AI analysis and extrapolation.

Recent findings suggest that you can also fully customize the VoicePad. The default configuration gives you quick access to your Calendar and AI apps, but you can remap each button to launch whatever apps you find most useful. You can swiftly pull up your email, image editing app, web browser or whatever you like with the tap of a button.

Dictation is often difficult in busy areas where there are lots of background noise, and in particularly quiet ones, where you can’t speak loud enough to be heard effectively. The SecondBrain VoicePad is built to work wherever you are and however you say it. Its dual microphones will pick up your voice even if you’re whispering, and they can pick you out from the crowd of background noise, too. That means you can take notes anywhere, whether you’re in a silent library or a busy airport terminal.

It has been revealed that only your voice and that of any colleagues present will be recorded, delivering clear written results, including names, numbers, and mixed languages. This is particularly useful when recording meetings between departments or across time zones, where different language preferences can make following along difficult. With the SecondBrain VoicePad you can feel confident that you didn’t miss anything in the meeting, with after-action AI minutes and notes making it easier to digest what was mentioned.

Sources indicate that most dictation devices need a laptop connection, too. Not the SecondBrain VoicePad. With 20 hours of battery life, you can carry this independent dictation device with you and rest assured it’s always ready to record what you need; No additional devices necessary.

Recent findings suggest that the VoicePad is designed to enhance the dictation experience with Genspark AI. If you’re already on Genspark, the VoicePad can act like your AI workspace right out of the box. Just tap the button and you’re off and running. Ask it to make a slideshow from your notes, create a full report, or bounce ideas back and forth with you. One dictated note can generate whole range of of alternatives for you to consider - fantastic for off-the-cuff ideation.

If you already use cloud-based AI solutions like ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, or Grok, you can link those with your VoicePad so all your AI requests are routed through those accounts instead. If you use multiples of them, you can even give each AI agent its own button, so you can send your dictated notes to the right one.

Not into AI? Don’t sweat it. SecondBrain VoicePad works just as well as a standalone dictation device and app launcher. It means leaving the AI features and support on the tablel, but even then the VoicePad isl fantastic for dictating emails, recording meetings, and translating international languages into something you can readily understand.

The SecondBrain VoicePad is now crowdfunding on Kickstarter with the campaign running through December. Super-Early adopters can get a SecondBrain VoicePad for just $119 - that’s $50 off its retail price of $169.

Each pledge comes with the VoicePad itself, with five customizable buttons, and unlimited real-time voice input, so you can record your voice with no additional cost. You get a year of unlimited dictation support, too, with 4,000 words a week free after that. Genspark Plus, Pro, and Team members can continue to enjoy unlimited voice typing and a free pool of tokens to use each day for transcription services.

It has been revealed that every SecondBrain VoicePad buyer gets unlimited translation service for the first year, too, making it ideal for multi-language meetings or travelling abroad with added confidence. After that 12-month period, translations cost a single credit per minute, but with Genspark credits priced at $25 for 10,000 a month, you’re unlikely to run out anytime soon.

The SecondBrain VoicePad is set to begin shipping in January to pledgees all over the world.

Show HN: Brickie – Deploy sandboxes in your own AWS account

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (342 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Github

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Brickie lets you run durable sandboxes in your own cloud / k8s cluster.
  • Brickie sandboxes are built on top of agent-sandbox with custom snapshot/restore implemented on top of object storage.
  • It has been revealed that each sandbox session is a container with a shell and a workspace and runs in your Kubernetes cluster with flexible runtime support, including Kata, gVisor and AWS Nitro.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Brickie lets you run durable sandboxes in your own cloud / k8s cluster.

Brickie sandboxes are built on top of agent-sandbox with custom snapshot/restore implemented on top of object storage. They are designed to be called from @hatchet-dev/sandbox and support the ability to take a coordinated snapshot of agent state. This means that every sandbox call is a retryable and observable Hatchet task.

It has been revealed that each sandbox session is a container with a shell and a workspace and runs in your Kubernetes cluster with flexible runtime support, including Kata, gVisor and AWS Nitro. Every call that changes the workspace produces a snapshot, which can be used to fork a fresh sandbox or resume an existing session.

Head over to the quickstart guide to get up and running your own Brickie sandboxes with a local Hatchet instance.

It has been revealed that brickie is in beta. Flags, chart values and the wire contract may change before 1.0. See the changelog.

It has been revealed that under the hood, brickie uses the agent-sandbox controller and warm pools to run sandbox pods. On top of this, the Brickie provider does a few different things:.

Every brickie sandbox turn produces an immutable snapshot in your object store, keyed by sandbox and Hatchet run ID. These snapshots can be forked into new sandboxes, or used to resume an existing session. On agent-sandbox, state is persisted through a PVC per sandbox, which forces a cold start, while the only point-in-time snapshot is GKE-specific.

Every call is a Hatchet task, so it is retried, observable, and replayed from its own snapshot. A retried call finds the snapshot it already stored and does not run the command twice.

The same code path runs on a Docker engine, so the Kubernetes cluster is not needed for development locally.

It has been revealed that pull requests are welcome from vouched contributors, and the first ones should be small. CONTRIBUTING.md explains how to get vouched, what to work on first and how AI use is disclosed.

Breaking: Crypto trading still forces consumers to choose between convenience and control

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (804 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thenextweb

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A candlestick chart on a dark screen shows prices sliding lower, mostly in red candles.
  • As security concerns persist across centralized exchanges, a new generation of trading platforms is attempting to make self-custody easier without recreating the complexity of decentralized finance.
  • According to recent reports, for years, cryptocurrency trading has involved a trade-off.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A candlestick chart on a dark screen shows prices sliding lower, mostly in red candles.

As security concerns persist across centralized exchanges, a new generation of trading platforms is attempting to make self-custody easier without recreating the complexity of decentralized finance.

According to recent reports, for years, cryptocurrency trading has involved a trade-off. Centralized exchanges offer relatively straightforward interfaces, but users must generally trust those platforms to hold their assets. Decentralized alternatives allow traders to retain control of their funds, although navigating wallets, blockchain networks, gas fees and bridges can make the experience considerably more complicated.

That divide has become increasingly relevant as security breaches and operational failures continue to expose the risks of centralized custody.

Recent findings suggest that the challenge for developers is no longer simply to build decentralized trading infrastructure. It is to make that infrastructure accessible enough for consumers who have become accustomed to the convenience of traditional exchanges.

Sources indicate that london-based cryptocurrency trading platform Byrrgis is among the companies attempting to address that problem. Its public launch on November 24 introduces expanded cross-chain trading functionality, token analysis tools and a simplified wallet experience built around a non-custodial architecture.

Sources indicate that on centralized cryptocurrency exchanges, users typically transfer assets into wallets controlled by the platform. While this arrangement simplifies trading, it also means customers depend on the exchange’s security practices, financial stability and withdrawal policies.

Non-custodial trading changes that relationship by allowing owners to retain control of their private keys and authorize transactions directly from their wallets.

However, self-custody introduces its own challenges. Customers become responsible for protecting their wallets, understanding transaction approvals and navigating potential vulnerabilities in smart contracts.

It also does not automatically eliminate exposure to third-party infrastructure, particularly when trading involves cross-chain protocols or external liquidity providers.

The question is whether developers can reduce those operational barriers without introducing new forms of dependency.

“Security and control over funds should not come at the expense of a simple trading experience,” remarked Siraaj Ahmed, CEO of Byrrgis. “With our full public launch, we’re bringing together cross-chain trading, token analysis and portfolio management in one place, while allowing users to maintain control of their assets instead of handing them over to a centralized exchange.”.

One of the persistent usability problems in decentralized finance is fragmentation.

In a recent development, trading assets across different networks can require separate wallets, native gas tokens and bridging transactions. Users may also need to understand which blockchain holds a particular asset before executing a trade.

Byrrgis is attempting to abstract some of that complexity through a trading interface supporting Solana, Ethereum, BNB Chain and, according to the company, Robinhood Chain.

Its cross-chain routing system is designed to let users initiate supported swaps with a single transaction signature rather than manually moving assets between networks.

A feature called Universal Gas is intended to remove the need to maintain separate native gas-token balances for supported transactions.

These approaches reflect a broader direction in blockchain development known as chain abstraction, where the underlying network infrastructure becomes less visible to the end user.

Yet simplifying the interface does not remove the technical risks of cross-chain execution. Routing systems, liquidity providers and smart contracts can still introduce points of failure, even when customers retain custody of their wallets.

Another challenge facing cryptocurrency traders is the amount of information required to evaluate unfamiliar assets.

Market liquidity, trading momentum and on-chain risk indicators are often distributed across multiple analytics platforms, making comparisons difficult for less experienced consumers.

Byrrgis has incorporated a feature called Scout Score, which assigns supported tokens a rating between 0 and 100 based on a combination of on-chain risk, market momentum and tradability indicators.

The scores enhancement as market conditions change, offering a consolidated assessment alongside the platform’s token discovery tools.

Such systems may make complex information easier to interpret, but they also raise questions about transparency and reliability.

A numerical score can simplify research, yet its usefulness depends on how indicators are weighted, how frequently data is updated and whether the methodology can identify emerging risks.

A high rating should not be interpreted as a guarantee of safety or future performance.

Beyond cross-chain trading and token analysis, Byrrgis has introduced card-based cryptocurrency purchases, a redesigned wallet onboarding process and changes intended to improve swap execution.

The platform also includes tools for tracking holdings across networks and managing multiple positions from a single interface.

These additions illustrate a wider challenge for decentralized trading applications: competing with the user experience of centralized platforms while preserving the characteristics that distinguish self-custody.

I’m always on the lookout for something newly introduced to add to my Netflix watchlist, especially when there’s a good mix of psychological thrillers, gripping dramas and a little bit of horror.

Thankfully, the streamer’s latest top 10 list has a few titles that have caught my attention, including one particularly twisted psychological drama that feels like “Mean Girls” meets “Jennifer's Body,” with a little bit of “Carrie” thrown in for good measure. If you’re anything like me and enjoy discovering your next binge-watch, these three shows deserve a closer look.

It has been revealed that leading the way is a provocative teen drama about a group of Catholic schoolgirls whose spooky initiation takes a disturbing turn. There’s also a gripping limited series inspired by one of the biggest financial scandals in recent history, following two ambitious young entrepreneurs whose relationship and business empire spiral out of control.

Finally, a lavish historical drama returns for its third and final season, with complicated relationships and plenty of royal scheming.

Recent findings suggest that note: This list is based on the Netflix U.S. top 10 shows as of Tuesday, November 24, 2026.

Netflix’s current No. 1 show is “The Body,” a coming-of-age psychological drama that’s perfect if you enjoy your teen stories with a much darker edge. It’s been compared to “Mean Girls” meets “Jennifer’s Body,” with shades of “Carrie” and “Yellowjackets” thrown in.

Creator Quinn Shephard and co-showrunner Gina Gammell have also drawn on their own high school experiences and religious upbringing to give the story a more personal feel. It basically thrives on early 2000s nostalgia, which leans into what Shephard calls “gritty camp.” It’s a raunchy, unsettling teen drama, and certainly a little different from your usual coming-of-age stories.

“The Body” follows a group of students at an elite Catholic school whose lives take a disturbing turn after a Halloween party goes wrong. When the school’s all-girls dance team welcomes a upcoming recruit, the group marks the occasion with an outrageous initiation ritual.

However, their night takes an unexpected turn when fellow student Grace (Sofia Wylie) falls into a coma. Anxious to avoid getting into trouble, the girls agree to keep what happened a secret. But when students begin reporting strange visions of Grace, rumors spread throughout the wider community, leaving the girls struggling to explain what they witnessed.

“The Altruists” is at the moment competing for the No. 1 spot on Netflix, and it’s easy to see why this real-life financial scandal makes for such compelling viewing. The biographical drama follows the rise and spectacular collapse of cryptocurrency exchange FTX, focusing on co-founders Sam Bankman-Fried and Caroline Ellison.

Their relationship takes centre stage as an $8 billion fraud scandal sends shockwaves through the financial world. The show actually draws on public reporting, court transcripts and financial journalism to piece together the events surrounding FTX’s downfall. Fans of “The Dropout” and “Inventing Anna” should definitely have this one on their watchlist.

Recent findings suggest that sam Bankman-Fried (Anthony Boyle) and Caroline Ellison (Julia Garner) are two ambitious young entrepreneurs who set out to transform the global financial industry. After meeting in Newly introduced York, the pair develop a romantic relationship while building their respective cryptocurrency businesses, with Sam at the helm of exchange FTX and Caroline running trading firm Alameda Research.

As their companies attract billions of dollars in investments, their growing empire brings them extraordinary wealth and influence. However, behind the scenes, questionable business decisions and mounting financial problems threaten everything they’ve built.

Stream "The Altruists" on Netflix.

Finally, “The Empress” is another great Netflix historical drama to add to your watchlist, particularly if you enjoy lavish period pieces like “The Crown” and “Bridgerton.” This International Emmy-winning German series follows the life of Empress Elisabeth of Austria, with plenty of romance and bold costumes along the way.

The good news for fans is that season 3 was always planned as the final chapter, rather than being cut short unexpectedly. Creator Katharina Eyssen wanted three seasons to tell a complete story with a proper beginning, middle and end, giving the series a chance to wrap up its characters’ journeys.

Industry observers note that following the devastating Sardinian War, Emperor Franz (Philip Froissant) returns to Vienna a changed man, struggling with the loss of thousands of soldiers. His wife, Empress Elisabeth (Devrim Lingnau), tries to support him while fighting to save their fragile marriage.

Recent findings suggest that however, Franz’s infidelity and growing tensions at court eventually drive Elisabeth to leave Vienna. During her journey, she meets Count Andrássy (Dejan Bućin), a Hungarian revolutionary who rapidly captures her attention. Meanwhile, Franz’s brother Maximilian (Johannes Nussbaum) travels to Mexico to claim the imperial throne.

Stream "The Empress" 3 on Netflix.

"We heard you like bass, bro, so we put a bass slider in your headphones to make them literally shake on your head. There's a vibration motor in there. Seriously, bro, they're so bassy. And $110 off".

In a recent development, sound, ANC, comfort, styling. These cans have it all. In fact, there was only one thing we didn't like in our Sony WH-CH730N review, and that was the U.S. price of $199 — way higher than the EU and U.K. relative pricing. Well, that's changed with this deal. For $99, the WH-CH730N are a hell of a lot of headphones for the money.

How about a very colorful pair of headphones for a great price? We're massive fans of the fit, finish and sound of the JBL Live 780NC, and this Black Friday deal makes them a great bet if you've got a little more to spend (but still want to maximise those savings).

The venerable Beats Studio Pro hit different when they're $120 off MSRP. Solid ANC? Check. A cool, stylish look? Check. Good sound quality? That's a royal flush, baby.

Bose might have replaced the QuietComfort headphones with (an also reduced pair), but at this price, these are headphones to go for. Excellent ANC for the price, a comfortable fit, and lovely physical controls. Not much more you could ask for.

Recent findings suggest that the Momentum 4 have a reputation of being a little... boring. According to recent reports, oh, look, boring raises its head again. If you consider 57 hours of battery life and excell... oh, I've made that joke before? Er... just buy the Momentum 4, not the Momentum 5. They're $160 and technically offer more battery life. Now that's no joke.

Sources indicate that sony's plastic fantastic weigh very little and sound excellent — and now you can get them for $100 off. Not that you should. Pure. Class. That's how I'd describe the Bowers & Wilkins Px7 S3. And I'd know, because I own and use a set of them on a near daily basis at home. Oh, and they're built like you'd expect from a luxury audio brand: bloomin' marvellously.

This isn't the lowest we've seen the AirPods Max 2 drop ($399)... but it's damn well close. And given these are the latest, greatest, and still rather new'n'shiny flagships from Apple no less, $130 is a surprisingly good chunk of cash off.

Look, I'm a Bowers fanboy, I'll admit it. And I own the Px8 S2. So I have no problem giving some sage advice here: buy the Px8 S2, you won't regret it. Yes, they're pricey, but they make up for it with beautiful, spacious, high fidelity sound, exquisite build quality and strong ANC.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone Duo have been out for quite some time now, and despite that, it’s still incredibly challenging to order an iPhone Duo in a timely manner. If for whatever reason you’re considering skipping out on this year’s iPhones, here’s what you have to look forward to next year.

2027 is going to be a relatively big iPhone release year for Apple. First, the company will be continuing the iPhone 18 lineup after it introduced a split release schedule. Then, in the fall, the company will debut a fresh round of flagships in celebration of the 20th anniversary of the iPhone. Here’s what to expect.

For the first time, Apple will be introducing its base iPhone in the spring. Upgrades for the iPhone 18 aren’t quite clear, though more RAM is one of the key rumors. Thermal upgrades will likely happen as well, as well as the new Apple C2 modem.

It’s possible Apple will patch the design to fall more in line with the iPhone 17 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro, though we don’t yet know.

This phone will of course equip the A20 chip, and it’ll probably start at the same $899 price point that iPhone 17 right now sits at – after it was increased from $799 in September.

This phone will most likely just end up being a chip bump from the A19 to A20 chip, and debut in the Spring alongside the iPhone 18. Earlier this year, reports indicated that Apple would share many components between the iPhone 18 and iPhone 18e, though it isn’t quite clear what that could mean for the devices.

It has been revealed that out of all of the spring iPhone releases, this one is the one to look forward to. After receiving a lukewarm reception with the initial iPhone Air model, Apple went back to the drawing board and decided to modify the design to fit an ultrawide camera into the device.

Personally, I don’t think an ultrawide camera is too crucial – though many people will see one camera on the back of the phone and immediately assume it’s less premium, so it’ll probably end up being an important upgrade for the sake of sales. Plus, ultrawide photos can be fun at times.

It has been revealed that it should also have a larger battery, reportedly as large as 3500mAh. That’s a roughly 10% improvement from the original iPhone Air. iPhone Air 2 will likely also jump from Apples C1X modem to the C2.

For the 20th anniversary of the iPhone, Apple is expected to debut a fully redesigned iPhone to celebrate. It’ll reportedly be much more glassy, feature significantly slimmer bezels, a quad curved display, and ditch the flat edge design of the iPhone 12 and later.

According to recent reports, personally, I’m slightly skeptical that this’ll truly be a replacement to the “Pro” phone for thermal reasons, but time will tell. iPhone Duo seemingly has strong thermals while not featuring an aluminum unibody, so my concern might not be relevant. It’ll offer two, larger display sizes: 6.4-inch and 7-inch. This largely comes from the bezel reduction.

I wish they prioritized the Telephoto camera more. I need that (whether it be on an Air or a Duo) way more than an Ultrawide.

If you’re holding out for iPhone 18 Pro, this “iPhone 20” is definitely the phone to wait out for.

In a recent development, lastly, Apple will release a successor to its just-declared iPhone Duo next fall. Of course, you can expect next-generation Apple Silicon with the A21 Pro chip next year, but there aren’t many other substantial changes expected. Apple may bring proper Face ID to the outer display, an improvement from the recently-announced face unlock, but it’s unclear whether this feature will make the engineering cutoff date.

In a recent development, its filing with the SEC before last week’s listing names the threat directly. It also warns that state-backed actors and competitors could pressure staff after they join.

According to recent reports, according to the Justice Department, D’iu photographed employees’ laptop screens in a coffee shop near the manufacturer’s Palo Alto office. The Microsoft logo on the side of one of its office buildings.

Sources indicate that microsoft has declared a “Code Red” to change how it prevents and handles major outages, Reuters reported on Tuesday, citing internal memos. The Microsoft Code Red follows the global outage of 12 to 13 November. It knocked out Exchange Online, Outlook, Teams and Copilot for about 24 hours.

Jaspreet Singh broke the story in a Reuters exclusive. Jason Henderson, president of M365 Core, called it the most customer-impacting incident in Exchange Online’s history. Never before had so many customers gone without email for so long, he told staff in a memo on Friday. The outage hit governments from Australia and Japan to the US, delayed trading firms, and disrupted airline communications.

“Code Red means that this is the highest priority work for our team,” Henderson wrote, according to Reuters.

Amanda Silver oversees M365 Core and Work IQ as a corporate vice-president. She described the response in a separate memo on Monday. Engineers worked through a “fog of war”, she wrote. Responders sent more than 11,000 messages across 11 Teams chats.

According to recent reports, diagnostic data sat in separate internal tracking systems. As a result, the team struggled to keep one shared picture of its theories and decisions, Silver wrote.

In a recent development, charles Lamanna is Microsoft’s executive vice-president for Copilot, Agents and Platform. He told a Code Red review that the failed part had seen “roughly ten years’ worth of acceptable failures”, according to Silver’s memo.

According to recent reports, microsoft has blamed a dormant July defect in Windows for the outage, a scalability bug that went undetected for months. Chief executive Satya Nadella apologised publicly. Microsoft says cyber activity and AI agents played no part.

Industry observers note that silver set out five workstreams under the Code Red, covering load shedding, splitting traffic by region, and faster recovery. Microsoft wants to resolve future incidents worldwide within an hour. It also intends to use AI agents to help engineers read system health data faster.

Industry observers note that henderson will hold daily meetings with the Substrate leadership team, plus weekly reviews. Substrate runs the engineering behind Microsoft 365’s core services. A Microsoft spokesperson told Reuters that its teams keep working around the clock to apply the lessons learned.

Industry observers note that earlier this month, Henderson wrote that urgent patches to M365 Core services took too long to reach consumers worldwide. In one recent incident, an urgent fix took five to six days. For the most urgent security concerns, he wants an hour from detection to safe worldwide deployment. Microsoft is not there yet, he wrote.

Last week, Nadella said that AI-found bugs will make outages more likely. Henderson also wrote that he had reviewed the organisational and structural problems behind the failure.

“Unfortunately, all the work we have done over the years was not sufficient to protect us on Thursday,” Henderson wrote.

#85403. Tech Report: How a Mechanical Watch Keeps Time (Interactive 3D)

📅 22 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1773 w)
📖 Baca
Gadgets ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Github ↗ Open Full Page

Tech Report: How a Mechanical Watch Keeps Time (Interactive 3D)

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1773 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Github

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Mechanical watches have kept time for 500 years.
  • This web page was partially inspired by Bartosz Ciechanowski’s Mechanical Watch page.
  • You can drag any of the 3D figures to turn them and see the parts from the side; on a phone, drag sideways.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Mechanical watches have kept time for 500 years. Many of their core parts were invented even earlier for giant cathedral tower clocks before being shrunk into portable timepieces. This page explains how a modern one works. I personally think it’s fascinating that a well-calibrated, purely mechanical device can keep time with 99.99% accuracy for $100. They also changed the world and look good on your wrist.

This web page was partially inspired by Bartosz Ciechanowski’s Mechanical Watch page. You can think of this page as a simpler introduction or background. When you’re finished with this, that page gives more depth.

You can drag any of the 3D figures to turn them and see the parts from the side; on a phone, drag sideways.

It has been revealed that start with the part that keeps time. In 1675 Christiaan Huygens, a Dutch scientist, invented the hairspring. It is a flat spiral of steel ribbon, finer than a hair. Its outer end is held still, and its inner end is free to turn. Twist the inner end and let go, and the spiral winds and unwinds, back and forth, at a steady rate. In this drawing it swings once every two seconds, and the rest of the watch follows that beat.

Why does a spring swing? Think of a diving board. Bend it down, and it pushes back: an elastic restoring force. Let go, and it does not stop at straight. It overshoots, bends the other way, and comes back again: it oscillates. With no friction, it would oscillate forever.

Industry observers note that A hairspring is a diving board rolled up. The board’s rest shape is a straight line; the hairspring’s is a spiral. Take hold of the slider under the next picture, and drag it to the right.

Industry observers note that “Bend” becomes “wind”, and “straight” becomes “rest”. Now give the hairspring a twist: drag the slider to wind the spiral away from its rest shape, and let go.

According to recent reports, it pushes back. It overshoots and swings, just as the board did. This one move is the whole idea of the hairspring.

The hairspring is only half of the timekeeper. The other half is the balance wheel. While most of its mass is around the outside, it is actually fixed to the spring’s inner end. The spring provides the restoring force. The wheel provides the mass and inertia.

A hairspring alone would oscillate far too fast to count. The wheel slows it to a pace that the gears can count.

Recent findings suggest that mass also makes the swing steady. Push an empty playground swing, and it jerks about. Put a child on it and it swings much more gracefully. A heavy wheel carries its own momentum, so a knock to your wrist, or turning it upside down, barely changes its rhythm.

How good is it? A well-calibrated mechanical watch, even an everyday Seiko or Citizen, is about 99.99% accurate. A day has 86,400 seconds, so that watch gains or loses about nine seconds a day.

Recent findings suggest that I’m not particularly handy with mechanical things. If I tried to build a table it would wobble because things would be off by a few percent. So it kind of blows my mind that, for $100, I can get a simple, everyday, purely mechanical system and tweak it to be 99.99% accurate!

Sources indicate that A second hand that just moves back and forth isn’t very useful. We need it to turn one way only. The escapement turns the swing into steps.

Recent findings suggest that the escape wheel is being turned by a mechanism we’ll explain soon, so it’s hidden on this diagram. Without something to stop it, it would just turn and turn.

In a recent development, its two prongs (called stones) stick in the wheel’s teeth: a tooth lands on a stone, and the wheel stops. Each time the fork rocks, one stone lets a tooth go, and the other stone catches the next tooth. The tooth escapes, and that is where the name comes from.

According to recent reports, what rocks the fork? The balance does. On its staff is a small impulse jewel, which sits in the notch at the end of the fork. It’s actually a synthetic ruby or sapphire, so it really is a jewel, a precious stone.

As the balance swings through the middle, the jewel strikes the fork and flips it one way. On the swing back, it flips it the other way.

So, at each swing, the balance lets the wheel take one small step. The step ends when the next tooth lands on a stone, hard enough to make a sound. This is the tick and the tock of a watch.

Recent findings suggest that before we go on, something that trips people up until they think it through. How long does the second hand take to go once around the dial?

In a recent development, each tick is one second, and sixty ticks brings it all the way around. So the second hand makes a complete circle once a minute. A hand is named for what it counts, not for how long it takes to make a full 360° turn.

In a recent development, the escapement gets the escape wheel turning at a precise rate. But the second hand must turn once a minute, and the escape wheel turns faster than that. To convert a faster rotation into a slower one, a watch uses gears: a small gear that meshes with a big one.

Industry observers note that the teeth on the two gears must have the same spacing, so they mesh neatly. Each tooth fits in a gap of the other gear, so the teeth go past each other one for one, and both rims move at the same speed. Four teeth on each gear are colored. Those four teeth are half of the small gear, but only a quarter of the big one. So the small gear turns twice for each turn of the big one: twice the circumference, half the speed.

Now attach the smaller gear (called a pinion) to the escape wheel. The gears do not spin freely any more: they move on one tick at a time, with the escape wheel. The escapement controls the speed of the whole train of gears.

Recent findings suggest that the significant gear pushing the small gear (pinion) is the force turning the escape wheel. What turns the big wheel? That’s a mechanism we’ll explain soon.

In a recent development, in this watch, the significant gear (called the fourth wheel) turns exactly once a minute: just what the second hand needs! So the second hand goes on the big gear’s axle. It is the first part of the watch that we can read.

The second hand turns once a minute. The minute hand must turn once an hour: sixty times slower. So we could try the same trick, and have a gear that’s 60 times bigger than the small gear.

In a recent development, but there’s a limit to how small you can manufacture the small gear, so the big gear would be huge. And it would have a lot of teeth which adds to the cost. Plus, it would turn the wrong way, counterclockwise, because every gear turns the opposite direction from the one it meshes with.

So the watch slows in two stages. The third wheel runs 7½ times slower, and the center wheel runs 8 times slower than that.

7½ times 8 is 60, so the center wheel turns once an hour.

In a recent development, the minute hand goes on the center wheel’s axle (arbor), in the middle of the dial. It makes a full turn once an hour.

The center wheel pushes the third wheel which pushes the fourth wheel which pushes the escape wheel. Next up, the mechanism that pushes the center wheel and powers the whole watch.

This is a spiral spring, like the hairspring. But instead of swinging back and forth, it does one slow unwind over a day or two. In the illustration above, it’s at rest.

According to recent reports, below, the outer end is held in place. Drag the slider to wind it up. The spring keeps its length, so its coils draw in toward the center.

Sources indicate that when wound away from its rest shape, the dashed line, it pushes back, as the hairspring does. A tiny one-way ratchet locks the axle (arbor) so it can only turn one way. To unwind the mainspring, let go of the outer end by pressing the button.

The block is gone, and the outer end swings around until the spring lies on its rest shape again. That fling is the energy that the winding put in.

A watch harnesses that force by attaching the spring’s outer end to a toothed drum called the barrel, invented by Jean-Antoine Lépine around 1760.

In a recent development, as the mainspring pushes the barrel, the barrel’s teeth drive the gear train we just built. This is the “hidden mechanism” we mentioned earlier.

Because the ratchet stops the arbor from turning backwards, the spring has only one way to unwind: by its outer end turning the barrel. Press the button under the figure, and six hours pass in six seconds. The barrel turns once, the minute hand six times, and the coils move back out to the wall. When the spring is completely unwound, the watch stops.

Recent findings suggest that the hour hand must turn twice a day. That’s once every twelve hours. Unlike the 60:1, a 12:1 gear is doable.

But the hour hand on that wheel’s axle (arbor) is off center! And it would run backward (counterclockwise): a pair of meshing gears turn opposite directions.

It has been revealed that so we use the same two-step trick we used for the minute hand. This time, 3:1 going out and 4:1 coming back. 3:1 × 4:1 = 12:1.

Industry observers note that the hour hand goes on the hour wheel, in the middle, under the minute hand, attached to a hollow tube (pipe) that slips over the minute hand’s axle. It turns clockwise, twice a day.

And that’s how a mechanical watch works!

Here’s a recap, retracing our steps in reverse, from the hour hand to the hairspring. The tour plays by itself, like a short film. The time scale in the corner states how much faster than real time each segment runs.

The hour hand is driven by a pair of gears totaling 12:1.

Industry News: Worshipping at the altar of Brendan Gregg

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that okay, I am the first to admit that I’m a bit manic with AI.
  • It has been revealed that I have been amazed at all the fun and useful things that a deterministic VM like Rewind enables.
  • Turns out that performance is yet another area where Rewind shines.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that okay, I am the first to admit that I’m a bit manic with AI. When you are working on a problem that has endless possibilities, it is difficult to constrain yourself to a limited set of features.

It has been revealed that I have been amazed at all the fun and useful things that a deterministic VM like Rewind enables. I have been using it to help find heisenbugs, to make profile-guided optimization reproducible, and to make Nix builds bit-reproducible. But the most fun has been using it to understand performance.

Turns out that performance is yet another area where Rewind shines. I have been using it to analyze the critical path of builds.

Recent findings suggest that the critical path is the longest chain of dependent work in a program. It is the minimum time that the program can take to complete, regardless of how many resources you throw at it. The only way to make a program faster is to shorten the critical path.

According to recent reports, if you worship at the altar of Brendan Gregg, you know he spent years turning performance analysis from a dark art into a science. This is a small offering to him. 🤲.

Industry observers note that I added a latest rewind time command to Rewind that analyzes a recording and tells you where the time went and what would make the run finish sooner. You can drill into any part of that answer and see the source lines responsible for it. It’s like Brendan Gregg’s flame graphs but on steroids for the critical path and with a debugger attached.11All the ideas for the command are either inspired by or directly influenced by Brendan Gregg’s work. Kneel before Zod!

In a recent development, aside: Newly introduced to Rewind? Start with a flaky build you only catch once and dafuq is a deterministic VM?

Let’s see how it works by analyzing the critical path of a libuv build and test run. The build and test suite takes 78 seconds inside Rewind, and even with 64 cores it still takes 47 seconds. Why?

Industry observers note that the usual answer is to look at a CPU profile, and in this case a CPU profile would be almost useless. For two thirds of those 47 seconds, the work the build is waiting on is not computing at all: it is asleep. 💤💤💤.

Every rewind time starts with two numbers:.

Sources indicate that the first is how long the run took on the VM’s one virtual CPU. The second is the critical path: the longest chain of work where each step had to wait for the one before.

No number of CPUs makes a run shorter than its critical path, so the gap between the two numbers is all that parallelism can buy you.

The line under the two numbers applies Gregg’s thread state analysis. Here the biggest state is asleep: 23 seconds in epoll_pwait and 8.5 in clock_nanosleep.

A sleeping thread is invisible to a CPU profiler. Gregg’s answer is off-CPU analysis: look at where threads block, not only where they compute.

It has been revealed that on a live machine, off-CPU analysis is hard. Linux can trace which thread woke which, and Gregg built wakeup and off-wake profiling on top of that, but you have to be tracing before the slow run happens, the tracing has a cost, and most of the sleeps you capture are noise. Rewind already logs every context switch because it needs them to replay, and now it records every wakeup and who caused it too. All that juicy information is in every recording. 🤤.

Here is the whole output for libuv:.

In a recent development, the second table is the path as a tree of processes based on Gregg’s colony graph idea. Each line is a process with everything it started, and its time on the critical path.22A ps snapshot might miss short-lived process invocations; the recording has every fork, regardless of how brief.

In this build, make check needs 41.9 of the total 47.4 seconds, and 36.4 of that is lt-run-tests, libuv’s test runner. The test runner invokes 287 tests each spending 1-3 seconds.

According to recent reports, all of those tests are on the path, and the path is a single chain, so the runner ran them one after another. Worse, most of each test is spent asleep, waiting on timers.

Drag can be less than time on the path.

According to recent reports, the last table answers a different question: how much sooner would the run finish if this part took no time? The critical path method calls this drag.

In a recent development, for the truly magical part, we can jump to any part of the path and see what was happening, invoke gdb and fork the run at that moment. A profiler hands you a stack, sampled at some moment you can never go back to. Every frame in rewind time is a moment in a recording, and Rewind can replay the run to it.

--in looks inside one process,33It can take a pid, a program or a word of the command line. so let’s dive into the hrtime test that spent 3.38 seconds asleep in clock_nanosleep:.

Recent findings suggest that since this test spent 100% of its time asleep, the step provided on the last line is where it began. rewind where replays the run to that step and asks gdb where the thread was:.

In a recent development, 🎯 We can see that the test is calling uv_sleep(45) from line 39 of test/test-hrtime.c, and that it is sleeping for 45 milliseconds. It does that 75 times for a total of 3.38 seconds.44Turns out that the test sleeps on purpose: it is checking how far uv_hrtime moves across a sleep. There is nothing to optimize in this case.

As the cherry on top: the run is deterministic, so step 115,894 is the same instruction every time you replay it. You can open rewind gdb at that step and investigate to your heart’s content.

The Rewind app’s Time tab reveals the same answers. The path becomes a flame graph, colored the way Gregg colors his off-CPU flame graphs: computing is warm, asleep is blue, and a process shades from one to the other by how much of its time it slept.

According to recent reports, clicking a frame picks it and moves the playhead there, so the build log, the process tree and the files all show that moment; clicking a process again zooms into it. When you pick a blue frame, the app replays the run to that part’s longest sleep and highlights the stack where it slept:.

Under the stack, Show source opens the source panel at that moment on that thread, and Open gdb here opens gdb in a fork of the run at the sleep:.

If you’d rather use tools you already know, rewind time can emit the data in their formats: folded stacks for flamegraph.pl and speedscope, or a Perfetto trace for ui.perfetto.dev.

The flame graph below is the real flamegraph.pl output: click a frame to zoom in, or open it on its own.

It has been revealed that every idea here predates Rewind. Gregg has been drawing off-CPU and wakeup flame graphs for over a decade, and build systems have reported critical path information potentially even longer.55Bazel’s critical path analysis is a great example of this, and it has been around for years. I have been inspired by his work since I first dabbled in eBPF, back when flame graphs were fresh. 🙇.

According to recent reports, what Rewind adds is the data. Lots of it.

In a recent development, rewind has that data because it can’t replay without it. On a single CPU the only thing that changes from run to run is the scheduler, so every recording already logs every context switch.

This changes the economics of performance analysis. On a live machine, you have to trace before the run, and tracing has a cost. You can only trace a few runs, and you have to pick which ones. Rewind traces every run, so you can analyze any of them later, and do so exactly.

It has just been a manic fever joy to take ideas I have admired for years, point them at a deterministic VM, and watch them work in ways that are hard or impossible on a normal machine.

Please accept rewind time as my offering at the altar of Brendan Gregg.

Kaszek closes $650M fund to back AI startups across Latin America

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Kaszek co-founder Hernán Kazah speaks on centre stage at Web Summit Rio in April 2025.
  • Kaszek Ventures has raised $650M for its seventh early-stage fund, which it indicates is the largest ever for Latin America.
  • In a recent development, kaszek Ventures, Latin America’s largest venture capital firm, has raised $650M to back early-stage startups building with AI, Bloomberg reported on Tuesday.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Kaszek co-founder Hernán Kazah speaks on centre stage at Web Summit Rio in April 2025.

Kaszek Ventures has raised $650M for its seventh early-stage fund, which it indicates is the largest ever for Latin America. It will back 20 to 30 AI startups, mostly in Brazil and Mexico, at a time when only 14 venture funds have closed in the region this year.

In a recent development, kaszek Ventures, Latin America’s largest venture capital firm, has raised $650M to back early-stage startups building with AI, Bloomberg reported on Tuesday. The firm says it is the largest early-stage fund ever raised for the region.

Recent findings suggest that the fund, Kaszek’s seventh for early-stage deals, beat its $600M target. Its last one, closed in 2023, raised $540M. Washington University in St. Louis and the Wellcome Trust are among the backers.

Industry observers note that kaszek intends to back 20 to 30 companies, starting at pre-seed and seed. It will keep about 60% of the money for their later rounds.

Most of the focus is on what Kaszek calls the “application layer” of AI. That means startups using language models in fields such as finance, health care and online marketplaces. Co-founder Hernán Kazah told Bloomberg he sees the most room in services for businesses.

Recent findings suggest that “It’s a more natural fit for the types of problems that exist in Latin America,” Kazah said. Many firms there still rely on manual processes, he added, and services can be costly or hard to reach.

According to recent reports, the fund is also looking at AI infrastructure such as data centres and chips. Kazah pointed to the region’s energy, land and closeness to the US. Power shortages, though, have held back data centres in Mexico.

Brazil and Mexico will stay its biggest markets, with Argentina and Colombia on the rise. Kaszek was founded in 2011 by former MercadoLibre executives Kazah and Nicolas Szekasy. Its portfolio includes digital bank Nubank, QuintoAndar and Kavak.

The raise stands out in a weak market. PitchBook ranks it the largest Latin America-focused venture fund to close since 2023. Only 14 venture funds closed in the region through September, it notes, against 68 in all of 2023.

AI startups can still draw big cheques, though. In August, Brazil’s Decade, an AI wealth adviser built by former Nubank staff, raised an $85M seed round.

#85398. Cento fine foods has been sued for “tomato fraud”
